_readme: Crop table for the plan builder. Data only — logic lives in harvest.mjs, beds.mjs, phases.mjs and frost/lookup.mjs.
Sourcing rules (see AGENTS.md): cite it or leave it out. Nothing in here may be a preserving time, a
pressure, a temperature, or a frost date — those come from the USDA/NCHFP guide and from NOAA.
days_to_maturity      typical days from transplant/direct-sow to first harvest (Johnny's, Fedco,
High Mowing catalog ranges). A planning estimate, not a promise.
min_frost_free_days   days_to_maturity upper bound plus margin — the shortest season this crop
finishes in. Filters crops against the REAL local season from the NOAA normals.
planting              plants per standard 4x8 raised bed (the geometry most people have), or feet of
row for drilled crops. Conservative on purpose: crowding is the beginner error.
unit is plants | row_feet for anything that goes IN a bed. Permanent plantings
(fruit trees, shrubs, sod) use trees | sod instead — they never take a bed slot,
bed30                 rows across a 30-inch bed and the in-row spacing, at the intensive spacing
Coleman uses at Four Season Farm (30-inch beds, 12-inch paths). Ranges are
'typical for the variety class' from extension guidance, not a published table.
family                botanical family, for rotation. Botanical, so it is a fact rather than advice.
method                transplant | direct | either, and how many weeks before last frost to start it
inside. Coleman's discipline is transplant-first: it buys weeks and beats weeds.
cold                  whether it stands into cold — feeds the winter-harvest list.
watch_for             the two or three pests and diseases that actually matter for this crop here,
from extension pest guides. This is what the scouting line is built from.
companions            widely described pairings; suggestions, not rules. The pest strategy phase
grades its claims separately (see phases.mjs).

crops.name: Tomato
crops.label: tomato bed

planting.note: 2–3 ft apart, staked or caged; fewer plants, better fruit

bed30.note: one row down the middle, staked; the whole bed is then reachable without stepping on it

crops.watch_for: late blight in a wet August, hornworms, blossom end rot from uneven watering rather than disease
crops.watering: Deep soak twice a week; keep leaves dry to slow blight.
crops.method_notes: The glut crop. Ripens in waves — the peak week is what the preservation plan exists for. Sauce, whole-pack, and freezing all work; the safe processing schedule is in the USDA/NCHFP Complete Guide to Home Canning.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-vegetable bulletins for spacing and pest lists.

crops.name: Cherry tomato
crops.label: cherry tomato row

planting.note: 3 ft apart and give them a tall stake — they get big

bed30.note: one row, and give it a 6 ft stake — it will outgrow everything else in the bed

crops.watch_for: blossom end rot, hornworms, splitting after heavy rain
crops.watering: Deep soak twice a week; keep leaves dry.
crops.method_notes: The fastest route to a first ripe tomato, and the crop children eat standing up. Rarely worth canning; eat them and freeze the excess whole.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-vegetable bulletins.

crops.name: Bush bean
crops.label: bean rows

planting.note: two 8 ft rows, seed 3–4 in apart

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart down a 30 in bed

crops.watch_for: Mexican bean beetle, bean rust in a wet year, rabbits while the plants are small
crops.watering: Even moisture while flowering and podding; drought = stringy pods.
crops.method_notes: Sow a little every two weeks to close the gap between flushes. Freezes well and pressure-cans well; process per the USDA/NCHFP guide.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-garden bulletins.

crops.name: Zucchini / summer squash
crops.label: zucchini hills

planting.note: two plants feed a household — seriously, two

bed30.note: one plant every 30 in; it will sprawl over the path, so put it at the bed's edge

crops.watch_for: squash vine borer (the one that kills the plant outright), squash bug, powdery mildew late in the season
crops.watering: Water at the base, deeply, once or twice a week.
crops.method_notes: Two plants feed a household. Falls off a cliff if you skip two days of picking — the preservation plan's real job here is the calendar, not the recipe. Freezes for bread; safe water-bath processing per the USDA/NCHFP guide.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-garden bulletins.

crops.name: Cucumber
crops.label: cucumber trellis

planting.note: grow them up a trellis at one end and you buy back half the bed

bed30.note: one row up a trellis at the north end — vertical, so the bed stays usable

crops.watch_for: striped cucumber beetle — and the bacterial wilt it carries, which is why row cover matters early; powdery mildew
crops.watering: Consistent moisture; mulch to keep the fruit clean.
crops.method_notes: Pick every other day once it starts. Refrigerator pickles and fermented crocks are the low-effort paths; acidity and processing for shelf-stable pickles come from the USDA/NCHFP guide.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-garden bulletins.

crops.name: Pepper
crops.label: pepper row

planting.note: 18 in apart; they stay compact and resent crowding

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart; they stay compact

crops.watch_for: aphids, flea beetles on young plants, blossom end rot; they sulk in a cold spring
crops.watering: Moderate, steady water; let the soil dry between soakings.
crops.method_notes: Slow starter in cool springs — black plastic or a row cover pays for itself. Freezes superbly; roasting and freezing is more practical than canning for most households.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-garden bulletins.

crops.name: Sweet corn
crops.label: corn block

planting.note: a block, not a row — a 4x8 holds four short rows of six

bed30.note: corn needs a block, not a strip — three adjacent 30 in beds minimum, or grow it elsewhere

crops.watch_for: corn earworm, raccoons (they know the exact night it's ready), smut
crops.watering: Heavy drinker during tasselling and silking.
crops.method_notes: Plant in blocks, not rows, for pollination. Freezes on the cob or cut off. Everything is downhill from the moment you pick it — pick and chill fast.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-garden bulletins.

crops.name: Beet
crops.label: beet strip

planting.note: two 8 ft rows, thinned to 3 in apart

bed30.note: three rows 9 in apart, thinned hard — beets hate crowding

crops.watch_for: leafminer (the blotches in the leaves), cercospora leaf spot in wet spells
crops.watering: Even moisture; the roots get woody if they dry out.
crops.method_notes: Root cellar and clamp the fall sowing — that is the whole trick. Tops are edible; don't compost them.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-garden bulletins.

crops.name: Carrot
crops.label: carrot rows

planting.note: three 8 ft rows, thinned to 2–3 in

bed30.note: four rows 6 in apart — the densest bed you will grow, and it works

crops.watch_for: carrot rust fly, forked or split roots from fresh manure, stones, or drying out
crops.watering: Shallow, frequent water until established, then deep weekly.
crops.method_notes: A late sowing left in the ground under mulch is the standard winter carry. Root cellar for the rest.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-garden bulletins.

crops.name: Kale
crops.label: kale bed

planting.note: 18 in apart; it keeps giving until the ground freezes

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart; it keeps going until the ground freezes

crops.watch_for: imported cabbageworm, flea beetle on seedlings, cabbage aphid in the fall, slugs
crops.watering: Steady moisture; tolerates less than most brassicas.
crops.method_notes: Frost sweetens it — this is a crop to leave standing. Blanch and freeze, or carry it in the garden under cover.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-garden bulletins.

crops.name: Lettuce
crops.label: lettuce patch

planting.note: three 8 ft rows, cut-and-come-again

bed30.note: three rows 9 in apart; cut the outer leaves and it keeps going

crops.watch_for: slugs (the real enemy here), bolting in heat, bottom rot in a wet spell
crops.watering: Frequent, shallow water; it bolts fast when stressed.
crops.method_notes: The one crop that genuinely likes part shade. Sow a little often rather than a lot at once — it does not keep in the ground and it does not can.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-garden bulletins.

crops.name: Swiss chard
crops.label: chard row

planting.note: 10–12 in apart; cut the outer leaves and it keeps going

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart; harvest outer leaves all season

crops.watch_for: leafminer, slugs; it wilts dramatically in heat and recovers fine
crops.watering: Steady moisture; it wilts loudly and recovers fine.
crops.method_notes: The most forgiving green there is, and it stands into cold. Blanch and freeze — it is not a canning crop.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-garden bulletins.

crops.name: Spinach
crops.label: spinach rows

planting.note: three 8 ft rows, 4–6 in apart

bed30.note: three rows 9 in apart; sow thick and cut young

crops.watch_for: leafminer, downy mildew, bolting the moment it turns warm — sow it early or late, never in July
crops.watering: Even moisture; it bolts fast when dry or hot.
crops.method_notes: The classic winter-harvest green — sown in late summer it stands under cover through the cold, which is exactly the Coleman winter list. Blanch and freeze the surplus.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service bulletins; Coleman's winter-harvest crop lists.

crops.name: Mâche (corn salad)
crops.label: mâche patch

planting.note: broadcast thinly across the bed and rake in

bed30.note: scatter across the whole bed rather than in rows

crops.watch_for: almost nothing — that is the point of it. Slugs, occasionally.
crops.watering: Keep damp until it germinates, then it mostly looks after itself.
crops.method_notes: The winter workhorse of the Coleman list: sown in late August it comes through the cold and is the first green of spring. Harvest whole rosettes with a knife.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds catalog ranges; extension bulletins; Coleman's winter-harvest crop lists.

crops.name: Leek
crops.label: leek row

planting.note: 6 in apart in two rows; dibble them in deep

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart, dropped into holes 6 in deep

crops.watch_for: leek moth, onion thrips; they stand through frost so they are a winter crop, not a summer one
crops.watering: Steady moisture in summer; they tolerate cold far better than drought.
crops.method_notes: Stands in the ground through the winter and sweetens — the other half of a Coleman winter. Dig as needed rather than lifting the lot.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension bulletins; Coleman's winter-harvest crop lists.

crops.name: Garlic
crops.label: garlic bed

planting.note: 6 in apart each way; the densest thing you will plant

bed30.note: four rows 6 in apart each way — 30 in beds are made for garlic

crops.watch_for: white rot — never replant garlic, onion or leek where alliums grew; leek moth
crops.watering: Water through spring; stop three weeks before harvest.
crops.method_notes: Planted in October, harvested the following July — the one crop you plant for next year. Cured and hung, it stores the winter; the harvest date is a calendar anchor for everything else.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-garden bulletins.

crops.name: Onion
crops.label: onion row

planting.note: 4 in apart in rows 12 in apart; sets are easier than seed here

bed30.note: three rows 9 in apart; sets are easier than seed this far north

crops.watch_for: onion maggot, thrips, and neck rot from curing badly — curing matters more than variety
crops.watering: Water until the tops fall over, then stop entirely.
crops.method_notes: Cure hard, store dry and cold, or braid. Sets versus seed matters less than curing — a badly cured onion rots in December.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-garden bulletins.

crops.name: Potato
crops.label: potato patch

planting.note: two 8 ft rows, seed potatoes 12 in apart

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart; hill them as they grow

crops.watch_for: Colorado potato beetle (hand-pick, they are not subtle), late blight, scab in limed soil
crops.watering: Even moisture through tuber set; stop as tops die back.
crops.method_notes: The storage crop by definition — the question is only whether you dig and keep or dig and eat. Cure in the dark, keep out of light.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-garden bulletins.

crops.name: Pea
crops.label: pea trellis

planting.note: two 8 ft rows up a trellis at the back of the bed

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart up a trellis at the north edge

crops.watch_for: pea aphid, powdery mildew, birds pulling the seedlings — net them
crops.watering: Water at flowering; wet feet rot the vines off.
crops.method_notes: The earliest real harvest, and it takes a frost. Freezing is better than canning for texture; pick young and in the morning.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-garden bulletins.

crops.name: Winter squash
crops.label: squash hills

planting.note: two hills, and let them run over the edge

bed30.note: one plant at the bed's south end and let it run into the path — or plant Blue Hubbard as a deliberate trap crop

crops.watch_for: squash vine borer and squash bug — this is the crop the trap-crop trick is for
crops.watering: Deep weekly water; ease off as fruit ripens.
crops.method_notes: Stores for months if cured warm and dry first — the basement is the preservation method. Two or three plants is more than enough for a household.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds / Fedco catalog maturity ranges; extension-service home-garden bulletins; trap-crop trial data for Blue Hubbard.

crops.name: Raspberry
crops.label: raspberry canes

planting.note: not a bed crop — give it its own 2 ft row and a trellis

bed30.note: not a bed crop — its own 2 ft row, trellised, outside the vegetable rotation

crops.watch_for: spotted wing drosophila (pick daily and chill immediately), cane borers; cut out fruited canes
crops.watering: Water during fruit set; keep the row mulched.
crops.method_notes: Year two is when it pays. Pick daily through the flush; freeze on trays and bag them, or make jam with a tested recipe.
crops.source: University of Maine Cooperative Extension small-fruit bulletins; nursery maturity guidance.

crops.name: Shallot
crops.label: shallot row

planting.note: sets 5 in apart in rows 12 in apart; four rows of a dozen

bed30.note: three rows 9 in apart; sets or transplants, same spacing

crops.watch_for: onion maggot (row cover before the 390 GDD flight, says UMaine), onion thrips in hot dry summers, allium leaf miner — not yet confirmed in Maine but spreading through New England, so scout for its leaf-puncture marks; purple blotch in wet years
crops.watering: Even, consistent moisture while bulbing; stop watering once the tops yellow.
crops.method_notes: A spring-planted cool-season allium: plant sets as soon as the ground can be worked in April, lift when the tops fall over, cure like onions. From seed, start indoors in Feb-Mar and set out early; Fedco's seed shallots run ~105 days and Johnny's ~110. Coleman grows them in the same 30-inch-bed system with tight in-row spacing instead of wide rows.
crops.source: UMaine Extension Planting Chart and 2025-26 UMaine allium IPM newsletters (pest GDD thresholds); New England Vegetable Management Guide (onion/scallion/shallot: transplants 10-12 weeks before setting, 9-18 in rows, 3-4 in in-row); Fedco catalog (Camelot: 4-6 in spacing in beds; Val-aux-Vents 105 days from seed); Johnny's (Innovator 110 days from direct seed, subtract 10-15 if transplanted); Coleman bed system per Johnny's/NOG.

crops.name: Scallion
crops.label: scallion band

planting.note: sown thick in four 2-3 in wide bands; thin to 1-2 in apart

bed30.note: four dense bands (2-3 in wide) across the bed, thinned to an inch apart

crops.watch_for: onion maggot (put row cover on before the 390 GDD emergence UMaine tracks), thrips in hot dry summers, allium leaf miner — scallions are a preferred spring host, so keep spring and fall crops covered if ALM is in your area; re-sow every 3 weeks rather than fighting any of them
crops.watering: Never let the soil dry during germination; steady moisture after that or the stems turn hot and stringy.
crops.method_notes: The easiest winter crop in Coleman's unheated zone-5 houses — one of his ~30 overwintered vegetables. Fedco calls overwintered Evergreen Hardy White 'a welcome treat in April': sow July-August for fall and spring harvest, April for summer. When bolted overwintered plants go to seed, cut the patch back to 2 in and it re-grows tender scallions.
crops.source: Fedco catalog (Evergreen Hardy White, 65 days, overwintering and cut-back advice); Johnny's (65 days from direct seed; sow early spring through early fall, extra-hardy types survive winter in well-drained soil); Univ. of Minnesota Extension scallion guide (direct-sow as soon as soil is workable, thin to 1 in); New England Vegetable Management Guide (2-3 in wide rows, mid-summer plantings for fall); Coleman, The Winter Harvest Handbook (scallions in the winter crop list, zone 5 Maine); UMaine IPM newsletters (maggot/thrips/ALM thresholds).

crops.name: Chives
crops.label: chive edge

planting.note: one row of clumps 12 in apart along the bed edge; it is a permanent border

bed30.note: a single row of clumps 12-18 in apart against the path side

crops.watch_for: Almost nothing — no significant pests or diseases per UW Extension, but two real risks: allium leaf miner prefers chives to any other allium (Cornell trap-crop trials), so a chive clump is the first place to scout in spring, and thrips silver the leaves in hot dry summers. Divide before the clump starves itself.
crops.watering: Drought-tolerant once established; a weekly soak in dry spells keeps the leaves tender.
crops.method_notes: The first green of the spring and a true perennial — one planting serves for years. Plant a clump per 12 in along the edge of a bed, cut back hard after flowering for fresh regrowth, and divide every 2-3 years. Fedco sells it as Maine-grown plants, hardy to zone 3.
crops.source: Fedco catalog (chives: 12-18 in spacing, full to part sun, Z3, Maine Grown, cut back after flowering); UW-Madison Extension 'Chives, Allium schoenoprasum' (no significant pests, divisions every 2-3 years, start seeds a few weeks before last frost); UNH Extension garlic-chives profile (80-90 days, full sun to part shade, Z3); Cornell/ESA allium leafminer host-preference study (chives most preferred); UMaine IPM newsletters (spring ALM generation hits chives first).

crops.name: Walking Onion
crops.label: walking onion patch

planting.note: bulblets 6 in apart in two rows 12 in apart; a permanent patch, divided not replanted

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart; bulblets pressed 1 in deep, 5-6 in apart

crops.watch_for: Thrips in hot dry summers (mostly cosmetic, says UW); allium leaf miner is the real one — a perennial allium patch is exactly where ALM overwinters, so a walking-onion bed can hold the pest for the whole garden: scout for leaf punctures in spring and again in September and cull infested plants
crops.watering: Tough once established; water only in extended drought.
crops.method_notes: A. cepa x A. fistulosum, hardy to zone 3, that 'walks': bulblets form on the stalk top, flop over, and replant themselves yards away. Plant bulblets (or divisions) in fall or spring; eat young shoots as scallions in spring, pull the strong underground bulbs late summer, and replant the topsets. No days-to-maturity is published for it — the 60-90 range is realistic field time from a planted bulblet.
crops.source: UW-Madison Extension (Mahr), 'Egyptian Walking Onions' (hardy zones 3-10, bulblets 1 in deep 4-5 in apart, thrips mostly cosmetic, divide clumps in spring); UF/IFAS EDIS 'Onion, Tree' (rows 12 in apart, plants 3-6 in); Cornell Botanic Gardens profile (A. x proliferum, perennial polycarpic, young plants used as scallions); Territorial Seed culture notes (bulblets 5-6 in apart 1 in deep, underground bulbs late summer to early fall). Not listed in Fedco or Johnny's catalogs — source is extension, not commercial DTM.

crops.name: Broccoli
crops.label: broccoli bed

planting.note: two rows of four, 18–24 in apart; one row of four is enough for a small household

bed30.note: two rows about 10 in apart across the 30 in bed; Johnny's spans 10–18 in between plants

crops.watch_for: imported cabbageworm (green larvae in the head), cabbage root maggot — UMaine's most destructive brassica pest: wilting plants mean check the roots; flea beetles on seedlings; clubroot where brassicas have grown lately
crops.watering: Even moisture; a dry spell at head formation makes small, loose heads.
crops.method_notes: The fall crop is the Maine crop: UMaine plants broccoli from late June through early August for September–October harvest, and Fedco warns spring broccoli has gotten harder as summers warm — heat makes loose heads. Cut the center head before the buds open yellow; side shoots keep coming for weeks (UNH). Coleman's transplant-first discipline applies; direct seeding buys nothing in a short season (Cornell IPM guide).
crops.source: UMaine Coop. Ext. planting chart (rows 24–36 in, in-row 24–30 in, plant 5/1–8/1) and 'Keep Your Garden Growing' (start 5–7 wks inside; early-August set-outs for fall); Cornell 2016 Organic Cole Crop IPM Guide (transplant, not direct-seed; 12–18 in in-row); UNH 'Growing Cole Crops'; Johnny's broccoli culture (DTM from transplant, +20 d direct; 10–18 in apart); Fedco broccoli (62–95 d from transplant; 'easier as a fall crop'); UMaine cabbage maggot & clubroot fact sheets; interplanting effect per Tahvanainen & Root 1972; Coleman, The New Organic Grower (3rd ed.), 'The Optimum Garden' (30-in beds, 12-in paths).

crops.name: Cauliflower
crops.label: cauliflower bed

planting.note: two rows of four, 18–24 in apart — one of the hungriest brassicas for space

bed30.note: two rows 10 in apart, 18 in between heads — it needs that room to make a good curd (Cornell: 15–24 in)

crops.watch_for: buttoning — small useless heads from cold or drought stress on young plants (Cornell: a 10-day stretch of 40°F highs); cabbage root maggot; imported cabbageworm; aphids working into the curd
crops.watering: Never let it dry out; drought or cold stress while young is exactly what causes buttoning.
crops.method_notes: The most finicky of the cole crops (Cornell): mature heads are not resistant to hard freezes, so in Maine it is a fall crop — UMaine's late-June through early-August plantings. Pick self-blanching varieties and skip the tying; purple and orange types never need blanching (Cornell). Give it the richest, most evenly watered spot in the brassica block and it repays you; skip it if the bed is short.
crops.source: Cornell Cauliflower growing guide (most finicky; heads not resistant to hard freezes; sow 4–6 wks inside; 15–24 in apart; buttoning from cold, variety choice for extended harvest); Cornell 2016 Organic Cole Crop IPM Guide (15–18 in in-row); UNH 'Growing Cole Crops'; UMaine Coop. Ext. 'Keep Your Garden Growing' (5–8 wks inside; early-August fall setting); Fedco veggie chart (transplants May, 24–30 in); Johnny's/Fedco catalog DTM ranges (early ~50 to late 75–80 d from transplant).

crops.name: Cabbage
crops.label: cabbage bed

planting.note: two rows of four; early compact heads can squeeze tighter, storage types want the whole 18 in

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart; early varieties can try 3 rows at 12 in, storage types want 18 in (UMaine: 12–18 in in-row)

crops.watch_for: cabbage root maggot, clubroot (UMaine: 4-yr rotation, keep pH at 6.8 or above), imported cabbageworm; mature heads split after heavy rain
crops.watering: Steady water; a heavy soak after drought is what makes heads split.
crops.method_notes: Grow two populations: early compact types for June–July, then storage types set by late June that ride out fall frosts — Fedco notes cabbage doubles its sugar after a month of cold, 'exposure to hoarfrost is good for cabbages.' Headed plants stand to ~20°F (UKy; young plants to 10–15°F for a night or two per UNH), which is what makes the storage class a November crop in open Maine beds.
crops.source: Johnny's cabbage growing info (early spring DTM from transplant, +14 d direct; 12–18 in apart, rows 18–36 in); Fedco cabbage culture (DTM from transplant; frost sweetening; early to storage types ~60–110 d); UMaine Coop. Ext. planting chart (12–18 in in-row, plant 5/1–8/1) and 'Keep Your Garden Growing'; UNH 'Growing Cole Crops' (12 in, cold tolerance); UKy NEP-249 (headed cabbage to 20°F); UMaine cabbage maggot & clubroot fact sheets; Cornell 2016 Organic Cole Crop IPM Guide (transplant-first; 10–14 in fresh market, 18–24 in kraut).

crops.name: Brussels sprouts
crops.label: brussels sprouts bed

planting.note: two rows of three, 24 in apart — the longest-season brassica and it grows 2–3 ft tall

bed30.note: two rows 10–12 in apart; 18–24 in between plants (Johnny's), row cover until June against flea beetle and swede midge (Fedco)

crops.watch_for: cabbage aphid — it tucks into the sprout and is hard to wash out; swede midge and flea beetles on young plants (row cover early — Fedco); cabbage root maggot's fall generation (UMaine)
crops.watering: Deep, steady water all season; a dry spell makes loose, leafy sprouts.
crops.method_notes: The patience crop: set out by mid-May (Fedco: start indoors no later than early April), then wait — flavor peaks after frost and sprouts harvest past the first snowfall (Fedco) or into December (Johnny's). Top the plants in early September when the lower sprouts are ½–¾ in for a uniform, once-over stalk (Johnny's, Fedco, UNH). Skip them if the brassica bed is short; Fedco wants ~9 sq ft a plant.
crops.source: Johnny's brussels sprouts growing info (DTM from transplant, +20 d direct; 18–24 in apart, rows 30–36 in; top at ½–¾ in; harvest after frost to end of December); Fedco brussels culture (very cold hardy, harvest past first snowfall, top in early September, 9 sq ft/plant, 90–110 d from transplant); UNH 'Growing Cole Crops' (18 in, frost improves flavor, pinch tip early September); UMaine cabbage maggot fact sheet (fall generation attacks late crucifers); Cornell 2016 Organic Cole Crop IPM Guide (24 in in-row).

crops.name: Kohlrabi
crops.label: kohlrabi strip

planting.note: about 6 in apart in four short rows — it is small, fast, and crops twice

bed30.note: four rows 6–7 in apart; Fedco short-season spacing is 6–8 in, Johnny's fresh-market thinning is 4 in

crops.watch_for: flea beetles (the main one — Fedco: row cover from day one), imported cabbageworm; bulbs turn woody and inedible if left too long
crops.watering: Even moisture so the bulbs stay crisp; drought makes them woody.
crops.method_notes: The fastest and most forgiving Cole crop: Johnny's grows it 'throughout the season in the North' and Fedco sows ASAP and again in August. Harvest at 2–3 in (Johnny's; storage types like Gigante to 8 in) — overgrown kohlrabi is the classic beginner disappointment. Coleman lists kohlrabi among his 30 cold-hardy winter vegetables (Winter Harvest Handbook), and Fedco's Kolibri wintered over under snow in Maine, so the late-August sowing carries into the cold months. Note: the edible bulb is a swollen stem, harvested like a root.
crops.source: Johnny's kohlrabi growing info (DTM from direct seeding, ~14 d less from transplant; thin 4 in fresh-market, 10 in storage; harvest 2–3 in; cool-weather crop); Fedco veggie chart (sow ASAP & August; thin 6–8 in, rows 12–18 in; Gigante 12–18 in) and Kolibri page (45 d; wintered over under snow in Maine); Coleman, The Winter Harvest Handbook, cold-hardy vegetables chapter (kohlrabi on the 30-crop winter list).

crops.name: Rapini (broccoli raab)
crops.label: rapini rows

planting.note: three 8 ft rows, sown thick and thinned to 4–6 in — a cut-and-come-again green

bed30.note: three rows 8 in apart, thinned to 4–6 in (Gulley: 6–12 in); sow thick and cut young

crops.watch_for: flea beetles on the young leaves, cabbage aphids in the buds; it bolts the moment it warms — buds open fast once weather turns hot
crops.watering: Keep it cool and watered; bolting is the failure mode, not pests.
crops.method_notes: Fast, cool-loving, and nearly pest-free in fall: direct-sow in April for spring or late summer for the fall flush, and harvest the budding shoots before the flowers open — expect a second and third flush over 2–4 weeks (Gulley). Coleman grows broccoli raab as a winter-harvest crop under cover (Winter Harvest Handbook's cold-hardy list); in open Wiscasset beds treat it as the earliest spring green and a September replant with a 2-week succession (Gulley). Early-spring direct sowings are the slow ones — up to 60 days — later sowings about 40 (IFAS).
crops.source: Gulley Greenhouse rapini culture (45 d; sow 4–6 wks before last frost and again 8–10 wks before first frost; successive sowings 1–2 wks apart; thin to 6–12 in; harvest shoots 1–2 in across before flowers open); IFAS EDIS broccoli raab (spring seedings 60 d early, ~40 d later); Fedco Quarantina broccoli raab (DTM from transplant; brassica culture, direct seed May/June for fall); Coleman, The Winter Harvest Handbook, cold-hardy vegetables chapter (broccoli raab on the 30-crop winter list); Tahvanainen & Root 1972 for diversified-planting flea-beetle effect.

crops.name: Napa cabbage
crops.label: napa rows

planting.note: two rows of four, 15–18 in apart — big upright heads; direct-seed the fall crop instead

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart; Johnny's direct-seeds 12–18 in apart in rows 18–30 in

crops.watch_for: bolting — young plants exposed to frost or a week of nights under 50°F run to seed (Johnny's); flea beetles and slugs on seedlings; downy mildew and black rot on the fall crop in a wet season
crops.watering: Even moisture from day one; stress while young is what triggers bolting.
crops.method_notes: A fall crop in Maine: direct-sow late July so it heads in cool weather (Johnny's direct-seed window is late May to mid-July; DTM is from transplant, add 14–21 days from seed). Spring attempts are the risky ones — frost or a week of sub-50°F nights on young plants sends them to seed (Johnny's). It stands light frost (Fedco rates Chinese cabbage 'moderate'), so the fall harvest runs into November, and heads hold 1–2 months near freezing (Johnny's).
crops.source: Johnny's Chinese cabbage growing info (DTM from transplant, +14–21 d direct; direct seed late May–mid-July, thin to 12–18 in, rows 18–30 in; bolting triggers; stores 1–2 months near freezing); Fedco veggie chart (Chinese cabbage: sow May, transplants 3–4 wks, thin 12–18 in, frost tolerance 'moderate'); UKy NEP-249 (Bilko 54 DTH); UMaine Coop. Ext. brassica pest fact sheets (cabbage maggot, clubroot); Cornell 2016 Organic Cole Crop IPM Guide (black rot, downy mildew in wet seasons).

crops.name: Buckwheat
crops.label: buckwheat cover

planting.note: Broadcast ~1–1½ oz over the whole 32 sq ft bed (2–3 lb per 1,000 sq ft, Johnny's green-manure rate) and rake in ½–1 in. Sow from after last frost until ~4–6 weeks before first frost.

bed30.note: drill 1–2 seeds per inch in rows 4–6 in apart (Johnny's), or broadcast and rake — the rows are just drill lines

crops.watch_for: Not frost tolerant at all — the first real frost kills it (use that). Mow within 7–10 days of the first flowers or seed sets, hardens and falls, and you get buckwheat volunteers (SARE, UMaine). It regrows if cut before ~25% bloom, so wait for full flower if you want it dead.
crops.watering: Water once to germinate; after that it's on its own — it wilts in drought but bounces back overnight.
crops.method_notes: The summer gap-filler, not a legume: it scavenges phosphorus (SARE: nearly 3x barley, >10x rye) and blankets weeds in 2–3 weeks, flowering in 4–6 weeks (MOFGA). Terminate at first flower — 30–45 days from sowing — turning in soft residue that breaks down in days; Coleman sows it through the frost-free period, ending 4 weeks before first frost (The Self-Fed Farm and Garden, ch. 6). Follow with a fall crop or fall cover immediately: it leaves soil loose and the released P can leach (SARE). It fixes no nitrogen, so plant it to catch nutrients for a hungry crop — but don't expect it to feed one. No same-family restriction for common vegetables; nothing botanical to avoid after it, only idle bare soil.
crops.source: UMaine Extension Soil Testing Lab 'Selected Green Manures and Cover Crops for Maine'; UMaine Bulletin #2270 (Maine Forage Facts: Small Grains); MOFGA 'Using Green Manures' (E. Sideman); SARE Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed., Buckwheat chapter; Johnny's Buckwheat Cover Crop key growing info; Fedco Farm Seed at a Glance; Eliot Coleman, The Self-Fed Farm and Garden, ch. 6 (sowing window, per Sustainable Market Farming review).

crops.name: Crimson clover
crops.label: crimson clover cover

planting.note: Broadcast ~¼ oz over the whole 32 sq ft bed (⅓–½ lb per 1,000 sq ft, Johnny's) or up to ¾ lb per 1,000 (UMaine), ½ in deep. Sow spring to early summer for a same-season green manure; sow by early–mid September to try to overwinter.

bed30.note: broadcast and rake in ½ in deep (UMaine) — rows are just drill lines

crops.watch_for: Winterkill in an open Maine winter — UMaine rates it 'not hardy in Northern New England', Johnny's says it only occasionally survives parts of Zone 5 with snow cover. Sown too early in fall it flowers before winter and dies. If it survives and you let pods mature, it volunteers. Deer browse it.
crops.watering: Water to establish the stand; once rooted it needs nothing until you mow it.
crops.method_notes: A legume, but in Northern New England treat it as a spring annual (UMaine): spring-sown it fixes ~50–60 lb N/A (MOFGA; SARE measured >50 lb N/A in zone 5b/6a trials) and reaches flowering in 70–90 days — mow at full bloom for the most nitrogen and the cleanest kill (SARE: full bloom kills it completely). Two honest Maine uses: sow spring to early summer and turn in by midsummer for a heavy feeder, or sow late summer as a winter-killed annual — it 'occasionally survives in parts of Zone 5 with adequate snow cover' (Johnny's), and if it doesn't survive you get easy-to-manage residue in spring (SARE). Don't follow it with other Fabaceae — beans, peas, more clover; and give 2–3 weeks before direct-seeding small seeds: crimson residue can slow germination of onion, carrot and tomato (SARE lab work).
crops.source: UMaine Extension Soil Testing Lab 'Selected Green Manures and Cover Crops for Maine' (crimson clover: spring annual, not hardy in Northern New England, 20–30 lb/A); MOFGA 'Using Green Manures' (70–90 days to flowering, 50–60 lb N/A); Johnny's Clovers & Alfalfa key growing info (⅓–½ lb per 1,000 sq ft; Zone 5 occasional survival with snow); SARE Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed., Crimson Clover chapter.

crops.name: Winter rye
crops.label: winter rye cover

planting.note: Broadcast ~1–1½ oz over the whole 32 sq ft bed (2–3 lb per 1,000 sq ft, Johnny's; UMaine 2 lb) and rake in ~1 in. Sow mid-August to early October in zone 5 — the latest-plantable cover of all (UNH); late sowings need ~2x seed (MOFGA, Fedco).

bed30.note: broadcast and rake in 1 in deep, or drill — rows are just drill lines

crops.watch_for: The spring escape: kill before stems elongate (UNH) — before seed heads in early to mid-May in Maine — or volunteer rye weeds your beds all summer. Late-killed rye gets woody and ties up nitrogen (SARE). Allelopathic residue can slow the next crop; wait 1–2 weeks after turning in (MOFGA). Avoid poorly drained spots (UMaine).
crops.watering: Water to germinate if the fall is dry; after that, never — rye's whole job is growing where nothing else will.
crops.method_notes: The scavenger and the organic-matter workhorse: the hardiest cereal, seeded later than any other cover, and the best net for leftover nitrogen — it holds 25–50 lb N/A over winter, up to 100 (SARE). This is Coleman's bulk-OM crop: rye with vetch over winter, turned under and allowed to decompose ~3 weeks before planting (The Self-Fed Farm and Garden; 'if he needs bulk organic matter, he grows rye and vetch' — Joe Gardener ep. 448). Sown mid-August to early October (UNH: even early October in southern NH), killed early the following spring — before stem elongation, ~early–mid May in Maine (UNH). Count on a short N tie-up right after incorporation (high C:N) and pair it with a legume (vetch at ~1 lb per 1,000 sq ft; Johnny's 70 lb/A rye + 30 lb/A vetch) or follow with a heavy feeder. Not a legume — it feeds nothing by itself. Don't follow it with wheat or barley: volunteer rye contaminates a small-grain stand (SARE).
crops.source: UMaine Extension Soil Testing Lab green-manure chart (90 lb/A, seed into late September, must be killed); UMaine Bulletin #2270; MOFGA 'Using Green Manures' (90–150 lb/A, mid-Aug to late Sept, mid-Oct in warm Maine spots, allelopathy wait); UNH Extension 'Cover Cropping for the Home Garden' (2022); Johnny's How to Grow Winter Rye (zone 5: mid-Aug to mid-Oct, 2–3 lb per 1,000 sq ft); SARE Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed., Cereal Rye chapter; Fedco Farm Seed at a Glance; Eliot Coleman, The Self-Fed Farm and Garden (rye+vetch over-winter).

crops.name: Hairy vetch
crops.label: hairy vetch cover

planting.note: Broadcast ~½–¾ oz over the whole 32 sq ft bed (1–1½ lb per 1,000 sq ft, UMaine; Johnny's 1 lb) and rake in 1 in. Sow mid-August to September 15 (UNH) — it needs 30–40 days of growth before a killing frost (Johnny's). Inoculate with pea/vetch inoculant.

bed30.note: broadcast and rake in 1 in deep, or drill (Johnny's); for support add ~1 oz winter rye (1 lb vetch + 2–3 lb rye per 1,000 sq ft)

crops.watch_for: Hard seed: any pods that mature mean vetch volunteers for years (SARE, NC State). Sensitive to frost heaving on bare ground (UMaine) — sow by mid-September or lose the stand. Kill it before bloom and you throw away most of the nitrogen. Slow fall growth means weeds can win if it's sown late.
crops.watering: Water to establish the fall stand; spring growth needs nothing.
crops.method_notes: The nitrogen engine of the rotation: fixes 60–150 lb N/A (MOFGA; Fedco lists ~100) — enough for corn, squash, tomatoes, brassicas. But it earns it slowly: sow mid-August to September 15 (UNH) so roots hold against frost heave, it crawls and vines through winter, then in spring wait for full bloom (mid-to-late May in Maine) — MOFGA: don't kill it until it flowers; NC State/SARE: ~50% bloom balances maximum N with easy incorporation. Mow to kill; tillage alone on viny growth is miserable, so mow first (Johnny's). Coleman partners it with rye (~4:1) for vine support and easier cutting; the rye offsets its own N tie-up with the vetch's N. Don't follow it with another legume — you've already made the nitrogen it would make.
crops.source: UMaine Extension Soil Testing Lab green-manure chart (1–1½ lb per 1,000 sq ft, 1 in deep, rye support at 56 lb/A, frost-heave caution); MOFGA 'Using Green Manures' (20–40 lb/A, sow mid-Aug, 60–150 lb N/A, kill at flower); UNH Extension 'Cover Cropping for the Home Garden' (sow by Sept 15); Johnny's Hairy Vetch key growing info (1 lb per 1,000 sq ft, 30–40 days before killing frost, 20–25 lb/A vetch + 70 lb/A rye); SARE Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed., Hairy Vetch chapter; NC State Organic Commodities (terminate ~50% bloom); Fedco Farm Seed at a Glance.

crops.name: Field peas and oats
crops.label: peas & oats cover

planting.note: Broadcast ~2½ oz of the mix over the whole 32 sq ft bed (5 lb per 1,000 sq ft, Fedco/Johnny's) and rake in ~1 in. Spring: sow as soon as the soil works. Fall: sow Aug 15–Sept 7 to winterkill (Coleman). Inoculate the peas.

bed30.note: broadcast and rake in; peas really want 1½–3 in deep (Johnny's), so rake well — rows are just drill lines

crops.watch_for: Spring-sown: mow at pea full bloom before the oats head out, or the woody oats are miserable to turn in (UMaine: 'can be difficult to incorporate') and the hollow pea stems won't mow cleanly after bloom (SARE). Fall-sown peas can survive a mild coastal winter — be ready to mow survivors. The dead oat mat keeps soil cold in spring (MOFGA); rake it aside for early crops.
crops.watering: Moisture at sowing for even germination — pea seed must not dry out — then nothing until termination.
crops.method_notes: The quick legume-plus-grass mix: peas fix nitrogen (90–150 lb N/A for field peas, SARE), oats scaffold the climbing peas, add biomass, scavenge leftover N, and — the point in Maine — both winterkill (UMaine PVO: not winterhardy; Johnny's: 'not frost-tolerant, a good option for a winterkilled cover crop'). Spring use: sow as soon as the soil works, mow at pea bloom before oats head, ~60–90 days (Fedco). Fall use, Coleman's Maine schedule: sow August 15–September 7, winter kills it, and rake the dead mat aside in spring to plant early crops without tilling ('winter-killed green manures... can sometimes be raked aside', The Self-Fed Farm and Garden, ch. 6). Peas are Fabaceae: don't follow with beans or peas. Mow before oats set grain or you'll be weeding volunteer oats; residue is low C:N and breaks down fast — good before anything except another legume.
crops.source: UMaine Extension Soil Testing Lab green-manure chart (pea-vetch-oats mix 150/30/50 lb/A, not winterhardy, difficult to incorporate); UMaine Bulletin #2270 (oats 40–60 lb/A cover, 30–40 days before first frost, will not survive winter); Fedco Pea/Oat Mix (5 lb per 1,000 sq ft, 150–200 lb/A, spring–late summer); Johnny's Field Pea and Oats key growing info (pea 5 lb per 1,000 sq ft alone, 3 lb in a mix; oats 4 lb per 1,000 sq ft; sow early–mid spring or late summer/early fall); SARE Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed., Field Peas and Oats chapters; MOFGA 'Using Green Manures'; Eliot Coleman, The Self-Fed Farm and Garden, ch. 6 (sow Aug 15–Sept 7 to winterkill, per Sustainable Market Farming review).

crops.name: Hot Pepper
crops.label: HOT PEPPERS · 8 · ripe=red

planting.note: 2 rows of 4, staggered at 18-24″ in-row with rows ~18″ apart. UMaine 4311: peppers fruit well when plants touch neighbors; skip 2 ft for access.

bed30.note: Two staggered rows ~14″ apart on the 30″ bed; 18″ between plants in each row (≈8 plants per 8 ft of bed).

crops.watch_for: Blossom drop and no fruit set when nights stay under ~55°F or over ~75°F (set after frost when soil is warm — UMaine: warm-soil crop, 5/25-6/20 in central ME); blossom end rot on fruit from uneven moisture, same cause as tomato BER; aphids (spread viruses); European corn borer tunnels into stems and fruit in Aug (a real NE pepper pest; slit stems, remove larvae); sunscald on exposed pods (UMaine 4311: sun scald + bird damage are the top pepper issues there); bacterial spot/anthracnose in wet years — pick resistant varieties (UMaine 2190 lists catalogs' resistance codes for peppers).
crops.watering: 1-1.5″/week via drip, even moisture; irregular water causes BER and blossom drop; avoid evening overhead watering.
crops.method_notes: Coleman program: 8-week soil-block starts (he germinates peppers/eggplants on bottom heat), harden off, and transplant only after soil is warm and weather settled — in coastal 5b that is late May to mid-June, and UMaine's own window (5/25-6/20) shows late is fine. Mulch the bed (black plastic or dark compost; Fedco recommends IRT mulch + row covers for heat) and don't rush: hot peppers love Maine heat if given a warm bed. Hot types ripen more reliably than bells; harvest green or wait for full red/orange color — UMaine: red/yellow peppers are ripe peppers, green bells are immature. Pick often to push more set.
crops.source: UMaine Ext. Planting Chart for the Home Vegetable Garden (peppers 18″ in-row, rows 18-24″, plant 5/25-6/20); UMaine Ext. Bulletin #4311 Sec. 17 (warm-soil crops, black plastic, peppers like to touch, sunscald/birds); UMaine Bulletin #2190 Vegetable Varieties for Maine (hot: Conchos, Numex Joe E. Parker, Thai Dragon, Tiburon); Johnny's 'Early Jalapeño' (60 d from transplant; sow ~8 wks before; 12-18″ in-row, or 2 rows on mulch 18″ between plants); Fedco Veggie Chart (start late March, 8-10 wks, 12-18″ in-row); UMaine Cumberland 'Sow Indoors' table (peppers 8-10 wks); Coleman, The New Organic Grower 3rd ed. (30″ beds, soil blocks) & Four-Season Harvest (heat-loving crops in coastal Maine).

crops.name: Eggplant
crops.label: EGGPLANT · 8 · warm bed

planting.note: 2 rows of 4 at 18-24″ in-row, rows ~20″ apart; stake or cage the tall 'Classic'-type plants. Dense but doable on a warm mulched bed.

bed30.note: Single row down the middle of the 30″ bed, 24″ between plants (UMaine chart allows 18″ in-row; Highmoor commercial trial used 15″).

crops.watch_for: Colorado potato beetle — UMaine calls eggplant a top host; adults and larvae skeletonize foliage, hand-pick orange egg masses from leaf undersides, and expect them (Highmoor picked CPB 41 days after transplant in 2023); flea beetles chew shot-holes in young leaves in June; tarnished plant bug deforms flowers/fruit; thrips scar blossom ends (Highmoor: 'Galine' badly damaged); verticillium wilt in old solanaceous ground — rotate 3-4 years. Plants will not set fruit in cool nights, extreme heat, or drought (Fedco, Highmoor confirm Maine-wide).
crops.watering: 1-1.5″/week, steady and at the base; drought stops fruit set and turns fruit bitter — Fedco: eggplant will not set in drought; drip + mulch.
crops.method_notes: Honest note: the riskiest of the nightshades in coastal 5b. Fedco: 'Growing eggplant can be a challenge in the north... some seasons even our skilled trialers get only sparse production of ripe fruit.' At Highmoor (Monmouth, central ME) even on black plastic the harvest window runs Sept 6-Oct 16. Give it the warmest bed, black plastic or IRT mulch (Fedco), row covers early, and short-season varieties from UMaine 2190 (Dusky, Black Bell, Neon, Little Fingers) or Highmoor's top performers (Annina, Classic, Picasso, Thanos, Gaudi — several with organic seed). Stake tall plants; pinch early flowers on young plants; pick glossy fruit before seeds brown to keep the plant setting.
crops.source: UMaine Ext. Planting Chart (eggplant 18″ in-row, rows 24-36″, plant 6/1-6/15); UMaine Bulletin #2190 (Dusky, Black Bell, Ghostbuster, Neon, Little Fingers, Kermit); UMaine Highmoor 2023 Eggplant Evaluations (seeded May 3, transplanted June 30, harvested Sept 6-Oct 16; top cvs Annina, Classic, Picasso, Thanos, Gaudi; CPB pressure noted); Fedco eggplant culture ('a challenge in the north... resent wind, will not set fruit in cold, very hot, or drought;' IRT mulch + row covers) & Fedco Veggie Chart (start April, 6-8 wks, 18-24″ in-row, 30-36″ rows); UMaine IPM Colorado potato beetle factsheets; Coleman, Four-Season Harvest (heat strategy for warm-season crops in Maine).

crops.name: Tomatillo
crops.label: TOMATILLO · 4 · staked

planting.note: 2 rows of 2, ~36″ apart, each staked or caged and pruned like a tomato. Two plants minimum — single plants set almost no fruit (self-incompatible).

bed30.note: One staked plant every 30″ down the 30″ bed (2-3 plants per 8 ft); unstaked plants sprawl 3-4 ft and need double the room.

crops.watch_for: Shares tomato/solanaceous pests: flea beetles chew young plants; hornworms defoliate (hand-pick or Bt); aphids; late blight can sweep through in cool wet Augusts (UMaine tracks late blight in ME); fruit rots where husks stay wet and crowded — keep air moving and harvest as husks split. Less disease-prone than tomatoes overall.
crops.watering: 1-1.5″/week, consistent; established plants tolerate dry spells but steady moisture keeps husks from splitting and fruit firm.
crops.method_notes: The low-maintenance stand-in for peppers in this set: vigorous, forgiving, and 60-80 days from transplant. Johnny's: plant deep like a tomato (adventitious roots), set 1-2 weeks after your earliest tomatoes, at least two plants for pollination, harvest when the fruit fills and splits the papery husk; husked fruit keeps for weeks at room temp, no processing needed. UMaine has no dedicated tomatillo publication — timing above follows its solanaceous-crop guidance (warm soil, transplant after frost). A 4x8 bed with 2-4 staked plants covers a family easily.
crops.source: Johnny's 'Toma Verde' tomatillo (60 d from transplant; sow 4-5 wks before; 24-36″ spacing; plant deeply; 2+ plants required for fruit set); Fedco Veggie Chart (tomatillo/husk cherry: start May 1, 4-6 wks, 2-3' in-row, 3' rows); UMaine Ext. solanaceous crop timing (warm-soil transplants, late blight tracking) as nearest UMaine guidance.

crops.name: Summer Squash
crops.label: SUMMER SQUASH · 4

planting.note: 2 rows of 2 at 30-36″ in-row (bush types); UMaine charts 48″ hills in wide rows, but 4 bush plants fit a 4x8 and a family rarely needs more than 2-3 plants.

bed30.note: One row of bush plants down the 30″ bed, 30″ apart (2-3 plants per 8 ft); Fedco sows 2-3 seeds per hill.

crops.watch_for: Striped cucumber beetle — UMaine's #1 cucurbit pest: chews seedling leaves, feeds in flowers, and vectors bacterial wilt which kills plants suddenly; row cover until flowering, hand-pick at dawn, transplant rather than direct-seed (Maine DACF IPM). Squash vine borer: frass at the stem base and a suddenly wilted runner; slit the stem and remove the larva. Squash bugs: egg masses on leaf undersides, feeding injects a wilt toxin — crush eggs, board traps. Powdery mildew in humid late summer (up to 50% yield loss, UMaine 5085): resistant varieties, good air flow, keep foliage dry. Blossom-end rot on zucchini with uneven water.
crops.watering: 1-1.5″/week at the base (drip), keeping foliage dry to slow mildews; consistent moisture prevents blossom drop and BER.
crops.method_notes: Fastest payoff of the fruiting crops — 45-60 days (Johnny's zucchini DTM is from direct seed; subtract ~14 d if transplanting), and it is the one worth successions: UMaine's safe planting window (5/25-7/15) allows a second, early-July planting that carries harvest into September as the first plants tire. Coleman transplant-first logic applies: 2-3-week transplants outrun cucumber beetles and start bearing weeks earlier. Harvest every day or two at 4-7″ (NE guide: 4-6″); one softball-sized zucchini stops the plant flowering. Companion: a 'Blue Hubbard' plant at the bed edge works as a perimeter trap for cucumber beetles, squash bugs and borers (CT/NJ research; UMaine 2190 recommends Blue Hubbard for Maine).
crops.source: UMaine Ext. Planting Chart (summer squash 48″ hills, rows 36″, safe window 5/25-7/15); UMaine Bulletin #2190 (Spineless Beauty, Zucchini Elite, Revenue, Space Master, Sunray, Cougar, Sunburst); UMaine IPM #5038 striped cucumber beetle/bacterial wilt + Maine DACF & ATTRA squash bug/squash vine borer factsheet; UMaine Ext. #5085 powdery mildew of cucurbits; Johnny's zucchini growing info (DTM from direct seeding; 'Raven' ~48 d) ; Fedco Veggie Chart (direct late May or 2-3 wk transplants, 2-3/hill, 4' rows); Boucher & Durgy 2004, J. of Extension (Blue Hubbard PTC on NE summer squash); Coleman, The New Organic Grower 3rd ed. (transplant-first, 30″ beds).

crops.name: Pumpkin
crops.label: PUMPKIN · 1 · vines out

planting.note: One plant per 4x8 bed, vines run out into the paths or lawn (needs 20-40 sq ft); small pie types can be trellised up a strong net with slings.

bed30.note: One plant per 30″ x 8' bed, 5-6 ft to the next; UMaine charts 48″ hills and Fedco 6' rows — inside a 30″ bed it is one plant, trained down the path.

crops.watch_for: Squash vine borer attacks C. pepo hardest (pumpkins): frass at stem base, wilting; squash bugs (egg masses + wilt toxin); striped cucumber beetle (bacterial wilt — cover young plants, hand-pick); powdery mildew (UMaine 5085: up to 50% yield loss; humid late summer; choose PM-resistant varieties); downy mildew can blow into Maine mid-August and kill vines before fruit colors (Highmoor alert, Aug 2024) — this is the classic 'green pumpkin in October' cause. Rotation of 3+ years for soilborne diseases.
crops.watering: 1-1.5″/week, deep soak at the base; taper off once fruits size up — a drier finish helps ripening and storage quality.
crops.method_notes: The reliable one in this group: 'New England Pie' (100 days) and 'Baby Pam' are Maine standards (UMaine 2190), and even jack-o'-lantern types (Howden ~110 d) finish most years. Coleman/Damrosch discipline: let fruit ripen and cure on the vine — harvest when the stem corks and the skin resists a fingernail; a light frost kills the vine but not sound fruit, then pull before hard freeze and cure 1-2 weeks warm before storage (UMaine Highmoor 'How to Harvest and Store Pumpkins'). Companion: a Blue Hubbard trap plant draws cucumber beetles and squash bugs away (Rutgers 2008 trial on pumpkin).
crops.source: UMaine Ext. Planting Chart (pumpkin 48″ hills, rows 36″, 5/20-6/10); UMaine Bulletin #2190 (Mystic Plus, Baby Pam, New England Pie, Neon, Baby Bear, Magic Lantern, Howden, Sorcerer); UMaine Highmoor pumpkin trials (2024 jack-o'-lantern eval; 2009 small-fruited pumpkin report; harvest & storage video); UMaine IPM #5085 powdery mildew (up to 50% loss) + Highmoor downy mildew alert (Aug 2024); Fedco Veggie Chart (direct late May or 2-3 wk transplants, 2-3/hill, 6' rows); Rutgers NJAES 2008 (Blue Hubbard perimeter trap for pumpkin); Coleman & Damrosch, Four-Season Harvest / The Winter Harvest Handbook (ripening, curing and storage of hard squash).

crops.name: Muskmelon
crops.label: MELON · 2 · trellis

planting.note: 2 plants trellised up a 6 ft net on the north side of the bed (slings for fruit); or 1 plant left to sprawl on black plastic. Highmoor commercial spacing: rows 8 ft, 18 in-row.

bed30.note: One row, one plant every 4 ft on the 30″ bed; trellis to steal vertical heat and air flow.

crops.watch_for: Striped cucumber beetle — the #1 NE cucurbit pest and muskmelon's worst enemy (UMaine 5038; NE IPM ranked beetle/bacterial wilt the region's top cucurbit problem): row cover until flowering, hand-pick at dawn; bacterial wilt kills vines fast once vectored. Powdery mildew (melons very susceptible; humidity-driven, resistant varieties exist); downy mildew reached Maine cantaloupes in mid-Aug 2024 (Highmoor alert) in wet years; fusarium wilt — rotate 3-4 years; aphids (mosaic viruses). Cool, wet summers simply don't ripen melons — variety choice is the only hedge.
crops.watering: 1″/week at the base; cut back as fruit ripens (dry finish = sweeter, firmer fruit) — Highmoor irrigated through plastic with drip.
crops.method_notes: Honest stretch in 5b, say so. Highmoor, central Maine, grows melons only through black plastic with drip, transplanted June 4-9 from ~3-week starts; even then mid-harvest lands late Aug to mid-Sept ('Goddess' ~100 d from seeding, 'Athena' ~115 d) and a cold year is a partial write-off. Use only early short-season types from UMaine 2190 (Earliqueen, Earligold, Fastbreak; 'Jenny Lind', 'Minnesota Midget' for heirlooms), plastic mulch, and row cover until flowers open (beetle barrier + heat). Coleman at Four Season Farm treats melons as a heat crop: transplants under cover early, uncover at flowering for bees. Harvest at half-slip — melons taste best when they come off clean. A perimeter Blue Hubbard trap is research-tested on cantaloupe plantings (CT).
crops.source: UMaine Highmoor Muskmelon Evaluations 2007-08 (plastic mulch, seeded 5/14-20, transplanted 6/4-9; 'Goddess' mid-harvest 100 d after seeding, 'Earliqueen' 107, 'Athena' 115; brix data) and 2017 ASHS trial (rows 8' on center, 18″ in-row, black plastic, ditched covers); UMaine Bulletin #2190 (early: Earliqueen, Fastbreak, Earligold; mid: Athena, Harper Hybrid); UMaine IPM #5038 (striped cucumber beetle & bacterial wilt) + Highmoor downy mildew alert (Aug 2024); Fedco Veggie Chart (start May, 2-3 wks, 2-3' in-row, 6-8' rows); Boucher & Durgy (Blue Hubbard PTC on cantaloupe); Coleman, Four-Season Harvest (Maine-zone 5 melon culture: transplants, heat, covers).

crops.name: Watermelon
crops.label: WATERMELON · 1 · stretch

planting.note: One plant per 4x8 bed, vines sprawl 5-8 ft into paths; hill 2-3 seeds or set one transplant on black plastic.

bed30.note: One plant per 30″ x 8' bed, 5-6 ft apart (Fedco: 2-3' in-row on 6-8' rows is commercial density).

crops.watch_for: Cucumber beetles (bacterial wilt) and squash bugs — same management as melon; fusarium wilt is watermelon's worst NE disease, soilborne and long-lived: rotate 4-5 years or grow wilt-resistant types ('Crimson Sweet' carries some resistance; catalogs list Fusarium races); anthracnose and gummy stem blight in wet years; poor set in cool, wet Junes; birds and rodents at ripening. Powdery mildew rarely attacks watermelon (UMaine 5085: does not commonly attack it).
crops.watering: 1″/week, deep, at the vine base; stop watering ~2 weeks before expected harvest — dry finish means sweeter, firmer flesh.
crops.method_notes: The biggest stretch in zone 5b — say so plainly. Fedco's 'Blacktail Mountain' (71 days) was bred by Glenn Drowns for cold mountain nights (~43°F) and is the Maine short-season standard; UMaine 2190's seeded picks (Yellow Doll, Sweet Favorite, Festival, Sunshine) are the other early group — skip Crimson Sweet-length vines. Grow every trick: 3-week transplants, black plastic, row cover until flowering, south-facing warmest bed. Even so, a cool summer yields few or no ripe fruit — UMaine Highmoor maintains no watermelon trial (their melon page exists; watermelon does not), which is telling. Harvest by tendril browning + hollow thump (Fedco's ripeness notes), not by calendar.
crops.source: Fedco 'Blacktail Mountain' (71 days, bred for cold mountain nights; ripeness notes) + Fedco Veggie Chart (start May, 2-3 wks, 2-3' in-row, 6-8' rows); UMaine Bulletin #2190 (Sweet Favorite, Festival, Crimson Sweet, Yellow Doll, Sunshine; note 'in northern Maine plant only early varieties of warm-season crops'); UMaine IPM #5038 (cucumber beetles) and #5085 (PM rarely attacks watermelon); UMaine Highmoor resources-by-crop maintains melon but no watermelon trials — flagged as evidence of risk; Johnny's/Fedco catalog DTM ranges for 'Sugar Baby' (~75-80) and 'Crimson Sweet' (~85-90).

crops.name: Arugula
crops.label: arugula rows

planting.note: 4 rows full-length (8 ft each) on a 4x8 bed; cut-and-come-again

bed30.note: 4 rows ~7 in apart across a 30-in bed; sow thick and thin to 2-3 in for baby leaf, ~6 in for full rosettes (Cornell)

crops.watch_for: Flea beetles (shot-hole damage; cover with floating row cover from the day of sowing); downy mildew in cool wet weather; bolting under heat/drought stress.
crops.watering: Keep soil evenly moist for fast, tender growth; drought makes leaves hot and hastens bolting.
crops.method_notes: Sow every 2 weeks from early spring until ~3-4 weeks before first frost (Johnny's/Cornell). Cut leaves ~1 in above the crown for 2-3 regrowth cuts (5-14 days apart); plants bolt in summer heat, so shade warm-season plantings. Self-seeds readily. Late-summer sowings are hardy in a hoophouse or under row cover — MOFGA lists arugula among greens harvestable through December in Maine.
crops.source: Cornell Garden-Based Learning arugula guide (spacing, succession, flea beetles, downy mildew); Johnny's Selected Seeds arugula key growing info; MOFGA Winter Greens (Dec harvest); Oregon State extension (40-50 days full size)

crops.name: Mustard Greens
crops.label: mustard rows

planting.note: 3 rows full-length on a 4x8 bed; baby-leaf band or bunching rows

bed30.note: 3 rows ~10 in apart; thin bunching types to ~6 in (Seed Savers 6-18 in); baby leaf: sow a 4-row band and skip thinning (Johnny's)

crops.watch_for: Flea beetles (row cover from sowing — Johnny's); cabbage worms and loopers in fall (Bt); bolting in hot weather — plant spring and late summer, not midsummer.
crops.watering: Even moisture for rapid growth; heat or drought stress makes leaves hotter and more bolt-prone.
crops.method_notes: Fastest brassica: baby leaf in ~3 weeks, full bunches 12-18 in in ~6 weeks (Johnny's). Succession-sow every ~2 weeks; in Maine grow early spring and again from late July for fall — MOFGA keeps mustards into December and lists them for overwintering under cover. Cut-and-come-again above the basal plate.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds mustard greens + baby-leaf brassicas key growing info ('Red Giant' 21 baby/45 full); Seed Savers Exchange mustard guide (thinning); MOFGA Winter Greens

crops.name: Collards
crops.label: collard plants

planting.note: 2 rows x 6 plants along 8 ft; big plants — needs the room

bed30.note: 2 rows ~15 in apart; space plants 12-18 in — collards grow to 3 ft tall (UMaine #4311) and are transplanted at 12-18 in per Johnny's

crops.watch_for: Flea beetles plus imported cabbageworm and cabbage looper (exclude with row covers; Bt for wormy leaves); clubroot in acid wet soil and black rot — rotate out of brassicas for 3+ years (Johnny's tests seed for black rot/black leg).
crops.watering: Consistent moisture keeps leaves tender; drought toughens them.
crops.method_notes: Not succession-sown — make one spring planting (transplants 4-6 weeks before last frost) and one fall planting (seedlings started May, set out June-July, per Johnny's). Harvest outer leaves from the bottom up; the plant keeps producing. Frost sweetens the leaves — UMaine #4311 harvests collards until temperatures hit the midteens and into early December in Maine. 'Flash' 55 days, 'Top Bunch 2.0' ~75 (Johnny's).
crops.source: UMaine Bulletin #4311 'Giving Garden' (frost sweetening, mid-teens hardiness, Dec harvest); Johnny's Selected Seeds collards key growing info + 'Flash' variety page; Clemson HGIC collards (spacing corroboration); MOFGA Winter Greens

crops.name: Bok Choy
crops.label: bok choy heads

planting.note: 3 rows x 8 plants; cut baby heads at 4-6 in for a denser early crop

bed30.note: 3 rows ~10 in apart; thin full-size heads to 10-12 in ('Joi Choi' spacing, Johnny's)

crops.watch_for: Flea beetles (floating row cover from day of sowing — Johnny's); premature bolting when seedlings get nights below 50 F or are rootbound/stressed before planting out; harvest before flowering; aphids in fall.
crops.watering: Even moisture at all times — any drought or setback stress triggers bolting.
crops.method_notes: Fast (~50 days) but strictly cool-season: grow as a spring crop and again from late July for fall — the fall crop is the better one in Maine, where MOFGA harvests bok choy through December. Do not succession-sow through hot midsummer (plants bolt); Johnny's advises sowing early spring through midsummer only in mild climates or with protection. 'Joi Choi' (50 days), 'Mei Qing Choi' are cold/heat-tolerant standouts (Johnny's).
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds pac choi key growing info + 'Joi Choi' variety page (50 days, 10-12 in spacing); MOFGA Winter Greens (Oct-Dec harvest)

crops.name: Tatsoi
crops.label: tatsoi rows

planting.note: 3 rows full-length on a 4x8 bed; baby-leaf band or full rosettes

bed30.note: 3 rows; baby leaf: sow in a 4-row band, no thinning; full rosettes thin to 8-10 in (Johnny's)

crops.watch_for: Flea beetles (row cover from sowing); cabbage worms and loopers (Bt — Johnny's); downy mildew on dense late-summer sowings; slugs in wet fall weather.
crops.watering: Even moisture keeps leaves mild and quick-growing.
crops.method_notes: Hardiest of the Asian greens: MOFGA keeps tatsoi through December in Maine and overwinters it under row cover or in a tunnel; Johnny's can sow it into late fall for overwintering in protection. Succession-sow every ~2 weeks through late summer (25 days to baby rosettes, 45 to full heads — Johnny's). Cut-and-come-again above the basal plate.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds tatsoi variety page (25 baby/45 full) + Asian greens and baby-leaf brassicas key growing info; MOFGA Winter Greens

crops.name: Endive
crops.label: endive hearts

planting.note: 2 rows x 10 plants at ~10 in spacing

bed30.note: 2 rows ~15 in apart; spacing 8-10 in encourages self-blanching hearts (Johnny's); direct-seeded rows thinned to 8 in

crops.watch_for: Aphids on young plants; slugs in wet weather; bolting and tipburn under heat (choose tipburn-tolerant types like 'Benefine' — Johnny's); seed goes thermally dormant above 77 F, so germinate cool (60-68 F).
crops.watering: Steady moisture — drought causes tipburn on the leaf edges and speeds bolting.
crops.method_notes: Transplant for earliest heads (3-4 week-old seedlings); properly hardened transplants survive 20 F (Johnny's). Succession-sow every 3 weeks. Days-to-maturity listed are from transplant — add ~14-21 days when direct seeding; baby leaf is ready in 4-5 weeks (Johnny's). Fall is the prime crop in Maine: MOFGA harvests endive into December. Maine-recommended varieties: 'Salad King', 'Neos' (UMaine #2190). Self-blanches when tightly spaced; force a cream heart by covering the center 3 days before harvest (Johnny's French technique).
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds chicory endive/escarole key growing info + 'Benefine' variety page; UMaine Bulletin #2190 (Salad King, Neos varieties); MOFGA Winter Greens

crops.name: Radicchio
crops.label: radicchio heads

planting.note: 2 rows x 10 plants; succession-planting to find what heads in your site

bed30.note: 2 rows ~15 in apart; transplant 8-10 in apart, crown planted slightly above soil line to discourage bottom rot (Johnny's)

crops.watch_for: Bolting, tipburn and bitterness under heat stress (UNH trials); bottom rot — transplant shallowly with the crown above soil (Johnny's); aphids. UNH found fewer than half of plants form marketable heads in a typical New England season — plant extra.
crops.watering: Even moisture, especially as heads form; dry spells cause tipburn and bitter leaves.
crops.method_notes: Treat as a fall crop in New England: Johnny's says radicchio grows best in cool weather (fall/winter/spring; summer only where nights stay below 60 F), and UNH variety trials (30+ cultivars) found chioggia types most reliably marketable with best disease resistance. ~80 days from transplant, add ~14 if direct seeded; succession-sow every 3 weeks (Johnny's). Seed germinates cool (60-68 F; thermally dormant above 77 F). 'Indigo' is Johnny's most sure-heading, tipburn-tolerant pick. Frost improves color and sweetness.
crops.source: UNH radicchio variety trial (NHPR/UNH 2024, Sideman et al.); Johnny's Selected Seeds radicchio key growing info + 'Indigo' variety page; Oregon State extension (~80 days, 8-12 in spacing); MOFGA Winter Greens (overwintering greens list)

crops.name: Sorrel
crops.label: sorrel clumps

planting.note: 3 rows x ~10 plants, thinned to 8 in; clumps spread wide over the years

bed30.note: 3 rows ~10 in apart; thin to 8 in in-row (Johnny's bunching: 8 in apart, rows 12-18 in)

crops.watch_for: Leaf miners tunnel in leaves (worst late spring through summer) — cut off and discard infested foliage and keep plants cut for regrowth; rust in humid weather; summer seed stalks lower leaf quality — keep them cut (Johnny's).
crops.watering: Even moisture; light shade keeps summer leaves tender (Johnny's).
crops.method_notes: Plant once — a hardy perennial (French type, zones 4-9 per Johnny's; MOFGA lists sorrel among overwintering Maine greens) giving some of the earliest spring and latest fall leaves. Days-to-maturity are for first harvest from seed (subtract ~14 if transplanting) — from year two it is simply there. Harvest outer leaves until established, then cut whole clumps above the crown; plants re-grow in fall even after bolting. Divide crowded clumps. Start indoors or direct-sow midspring through midsummer (Johnny's).
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds sorrel key growing info + 'Sorrel' (French type) variety page; MOFGA Winter Greens (overwintering greens list)

crops.name: Basil
crops.label: basil block

planting.note: 4-8 in apart (Johnny's); 16 plants in two 8-ft rows; pinch tips to force branching

bed30.note: three rows across a 30 in bed, 8 in in-row (Johnny's 4-8 in); cut whole plants 4-6 in above ground for a second flush

crops.watch_for: BASIL DOWNY MILDEW — the big one in the Northeast since 2007 (yellowing between veins, grey spores under leaves; wind-borne, doesn't overwinter here, Cornell/UConn); Japanese beetles; fusarium wilt
crops.watering: Regular moisture — basil is not drought tolerant (Johnny's); water the soil, keep leaves dry to slow downy mildew.
crops.method_notes: Warm-season ANNUAL — never out until nights stay above 50°F (Johnny's). Coleman-style: transplant-first at 6 weeks, dense spacing, and pinch the growing tip once plants are 6-8 in for a low, leafy plant. Harvest before flowering by cutting back to a pair of side shoots; strip flower buds to hold the window open. UMaine's Maine Home Garden News puts basil with the tender plants set out in June, and with tomatoes in the same bed is the classic pairing.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Genovese 68 d, 4-8 in spacing, sow 6 wk indoors); Cornell vegetables and UConn IPM basil downy mildew factsheets; UMaine Maine Home Garden News June 2025 (tender annuals; basil+tomato).

crops.name: Dill
crops.label: dill row

planting.note: sow two 8-ft rows, 1/4 in deep; thinning barely needed if you harvest leaves young

bed30.note: three rows across a 30 in bed sown thin; Johnny's says thinning is not necessary for leaf harvest

crops.watch_for: BOLTING — dill 'bolts quickly in hot conditions' (Johnny's); sow early and in successions rather than fighting July; parsleyworm (black swallowtail caterpillar — let it eat, it becomes a butterfly); aphids
crops.watering: Even moisture; don't let young plants dry out or they rush to seed.
crops.method_notes: Cool-season ANNUAL; direct-sow as soon as the soil can be worked and again every ~3 weeks (Johnny's) to keep leaf coming. In the bed system it is as much insectary as herb: UMaine (MHGN June 2025) and UNH's insectary-plant research both place flowering dill among the top hoverfly attractants — hoverfly larvae eat aphids — and UMaine notes dill draws tiger swallowtails. Let every third plant flower rather than stripping it, and it pays the bed back.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Bouquet 40-45 d to leaf, 85-105 d to seed; succession sowings every 3 wk); Fedco (Bouquet 55 d, 'especially attractive to pollinators'); UMaine MHGN June 2025 (hoverflies, let herbs flower); UNH Extension insectary-plant research report 2017-18.

crops.name: Parsley
crops.label: parsley row

planting.note: 12 plants ~9 in apart; seeds germinate notoriously slowly (14-30 d, Johnny's), so start early

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart; Johnny's thins direct-sown parsley to 8-12 in

crops.watch_for: parsleyworm (black swallowtail caterpillar), Septoria leaf spot in wet spells, and second-year bolting — it is a biennial and wants to flower year two
crops.watering: Moist, fertile soil; clip outer leaves and it keeps producing all season.
crops.method_notes: COOL-season biennial grown as an annual but a real winter survivor: Johnny's notes parsley 'wintered over' in a well-drained spot gives an early spring crop (mulch where it goes below 0°F), and parsley is on Eliot Coleman's list of ~30 cold-hardy crops grown through winter in the unheated greenhouses of the Winter Harvest Handbook. Slow germination is the whole trick — start indoors ~9-10 weeks (Johnny's) or soak patience. Establish by August for winter use.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Giant of Italy 75 d; germ 14-30 d; winter-over & mulch notes; 9-10 wk indoor start); Eliot Coleman, The Winter Harvest Handbook (parsley among cold-hardy winter greenhouse crops, ch. 8); extension parsley maturity ~70-90 d.

crops.name: Cilantro
crops.label: cilantro strip

planting.note: two 8-ft rows sown 1/4 in deep; keeps better in cool weather than summer heat

bed30.note: three rows, 4 in in-row; it is a leaf crop, so density is fine

crops.watch_for: BOLTING — cilantro 'bolts quickly in hot conditions' (Johnny's); heat and long days trigger it, so the crop is spring and fall, not July; aphids on new growth
crops.watering: Steady moisture, lighter afternoon shade in heat; drought = instant bolting.
crops.method_notes: Cool-season ANNUAL, the fastest leaf herb in the bed. Direct-sow in successions every 2 weeks and pull whole plants when leaves are full. UNH's insectary research found cilantro among the top hoverfly attractants of the plants tested, so let a few plants flower for the bed even as you strip the rest. If you want coriander seed, stop picking and it will set seed ~90-105 days in.
crops.source: Fedco (Caribe & Leisure 55 d; Longstanding 30 d leaf / 45 d seed, 'grows best in cool temperatures'); Johnny's (bolting note; succession practice); UNH Extension insectary-plant research report 2017-18 (cilantro among top hoverfly attractants).

crops.name: Thyme
crops.label: thyme edge

planting.note: 16 plants at 6-8 in (Johnny's) — small, low, and happy at the bed edge

bed30.note: three rows at 8 in; thyme stays short and spreads, so it also works as the bed's front edging

crops.watch_for: WINTERKILL in wet, poorly drained beds — Johnny's advises cutting only a few stems the first year 'in order for the plants to winter over'; root rot in soggy soil; spider mites in summer drought
crops.watering: Dry, well-drained soil and little water — it sulks in wet feet.
crops.method_notes: MARGINALLY HARDIY perennial in zone 5b — reliable only in the driest, best-drained bed (or gravel); treat the first year gently to get it through winter (Johnny's). Seed is slow (90-95 d, Johnny's) so transplant, and pinch tips for bushiness. Thyme goes woody and needs division or replacement after 3-4 years (Johnny's). UMaine's bee research clocked garden thyme among the most-visited herbs in Maine.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (German Winter 90-95 d; 8-10 wk indoor start; light first-year harvest to winter over; woody after 3-4 yr); UMaine Bulletin #2076, Selecting Plants to Support Bees in Maine (garden thyme, high June visitation).

crops.name: Oregano
crops.label: oregano row

planting.note: 8 plants at 12 in (Johnny's); it sprawls, so give it room

bed30.note: two rows at 12 in; cut back after flowering to keep it tidy

crops.watch_for: aphids on new growth; root rot in heavy wet soil — otherwise about the easiest herb in Maine; divide every few years as the center dies out
crops.watering: Likes it dry once established; water only in long drought.
crops.method_notes: RELIABLY HARDIY perennial in zone 5b; Greek oregano is the culinary one. UMaine's four-year bee study (Bulletin #2076) counted oregano among the most-visited, longest-flowering bee plants of everything tested — a flowering oregano plant is doing pollinator duty for the bee-pollinated crops in the beds around it. Slow from seed (Johnny's 8-10 wk indoors); harvest just as flowers begin to open.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (oregano 80-90 d; 8-10 wk indoor start); UMaine Bulletin #2076 (oregano among most-visited bee plants, Greek oregano photographed with bumble bee); UMaine MHGN June 2025 (oregano with tomatoes).

crops.name: Sage
crops.label: sage corner

planting.note: 4 plants at 12-18 in (Johnny's 12 in) — it becomes a 16-30 in woody shrub

bed30.note: two rows at 15 in; give it a corner or bed end so it doesn't shade leafy neighbors

crops.watch_for: winterkill in wet heavy soil (sage wants sharp drainage); spider mites in drought; plants go woody and are best replaced every few years (Johnny's)
crops.watering: Very drought-tolerant; water only in extended dry spells.
crops.method_notes: RELIABLY HARDIY perennial in zone 5b (Johnny's lists zones 4-8), but it rots in wet winters, so put it in the sandiest bed corner. Classic companion-planting pairing with carrots and the cabbage family; starts slowly from seed (6-8 wk inside, Johnny's), so buying one plant or taking divisions is the fast route. Cut stems as flowers start to open for the strongest flavor.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Common Sage 80-90 d; 6-8 wk indoor start; zones 4-8; spacing 12 in; woody replacement note); classic companion lists (Burpee: sage with cabbage family & carrots); UMaine MHGN June 2025 lists sage among pollinator-friendly herbs.

crops.name: Rosemary
crops.label: rosemary pot

planting.note: 4 plants at 8-10 in when grown as an annual (Johnny's); it wants warmth and sharp drainage

bed30.note: two rows at 12 in; Johnny's: plant 8-10 in apart as an annual, 24-36 in only if it overwinters

crops.watch_for: ROOT ROT from wet feet (its #1 killer in Maine; Johnny's wants well-drained soil); powdery mildew and spider mites when overwintered indoors
crops.watering: Let the soil dry between waterings; never soggy, and keep it warm — it sulks below 50°F.
crops.method_notes: TENDER PERENNIAL in zone 5b — Johnny's lists it zones 6-10, and UMaine's Maine Home Garden News groups rosemary with the tender perennials you grow as annuals here (or overwinter in a pot in a sunny window). Slow from seed (10-12 wk inside, Johnny's); many Maine gardeners just buy a plant. Harvest of stem tips begins ~80-100 days from planting (Johnny's). In the bean bed, old companion lists credit it with deterring bean beetles.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (rosemary 10-12 wk indoor start; zones 6-10; 80-100 d to first harvest; 8-10 in as annual spacing); UMaine Maine Home Garden News June 2025 (rosemary among tender perennials grown as annuals, pollinator-friendly); Burpee companion chart (rosemary deters bean beetles).

crops.name: Mint
crops.label: mint tub

planting.note: 4 plants at 12-18 in (Johnny's) — but ONLY in a sunken tub or barrier; see method_notes

bed30.note: two rows, but plan for the runner: a buried pot or edging barrier is mandatory or mint owns the bed in one season

crops.watch_for: MINT RUST (Puccinia menthae — orange pustules under leaves; also infects marjoram and savory, per RHS) — cut out infected shoots before spores blacken; aphids; spider mites in drought
crops.watering: Moist soil is fine, but water the soil in the morning and never overhead — wet leaves invite rust.
crops.method_notes: RELIABLY HARDIY perennial in zone 5b (Johnny's: zones 4-9), and the one herb that must be CONTAINED: Johnny's own culture notes warn it 'may become invasive in the field.' Coleman and Damrosch plant mints in sunken pots or dedicated beds with barriers — planted bare in a 30-in bed it will colonize half the garden by August.
