Young transplants withstand some freezing (Johnny's) so it goes out early. Rust management is the only real chore: thin stems for airflow, remove spotted shoots, don't compost them.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Common mint 70-80 d; zones 4-9; 6-8 wk indoor start; 'may become invasive in field'); RHS mint rust (Puccinia menthae; also infects marjoram & savory); PNW Pest Management Handbooks (Mentha rust); Coleman/Damrosch bed practice (contained planting).

crops.name: French Tarragon
crops.label: tarragon corner

planting.note: 4 divisions at 12-18 in; propagate by spring root divisions or cuttings — NEVER from seed

bed30.note: two rows at 15 in in the driest corner of the bed

crops.watch_for: WINTERKILL — hardy to zone 4 per USU, but crowns rot in wet Maine winters, so plant in the best-drained spot and mulch the crown; aphids; spider mites in drought
crops.watering: Dry and lean — too much water kills it faster than cold does.
crops.method_notes: MARGINALLY HARDIY perennial in zone 5b. The essential fact: TRUE FRENCH TARRAGON IS A STERILE CLONE — it sets no viable seed, so anything grown from seed is Russian tarragon, which is nearly flavorless (USU Extension). Buy a plant, then propagate it by spring root divisions or stem cuttings (USU). The 90-120 day figure is an honest estimate to a full first picking from a spring division — no seed catalog lists a days-to-maturity because none sell true French tarragon seed. Divide every 3-4 years to keep flavor strong.
crops.source: Utah State University Extension, French Tarragon in the Garden (sterile clone; divisions/cuttings only; winter hardy to zone 4; Russian tarragon from seed is flavorless); no catalog DTM exists — 90-120 d estimated from a spring division.

crops.name: Summer savory
crops.label: savory edge

planting.note: 12 plants at 6-8 in; direct-sow or set out after frost

bed30.note: three rows at 8 in; it stays a tidy 12 in and finishes fast

crops.watch_for: mostly pest-free — occasional aphids; if it bolts in a heat wave, cut it back and it resprouts from the base
crops.watering: Even moisture while young; drought-tolerant once growing.
crops.method_notes: COOL-season ANNUAL with real frost tolerance — a late-summer sowing gives a fall crop (UMaine lists summer savory with the sturdy herbs that dry easily; classic companion charts put it at the base of bean plants to deter Mexican bean beetles and improve bean flavor — Burpee's chart spells out both). It is the annual stand-in for winter savory, which is a perennial (Fedco) but stronger and coarser-flavored.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Summer Savory 60-70 d); Burpee companion chart (summer savory deters bean beetles, improves growth & flavor of beans; also an onion ally); Fedco (winter savory, Satureja montana, 100 d perennial, 'stronger and more pungent').

crops.name: Bulb fennel
crops.label: fennel row

planting.note: 8 plants at 6 in (Johnny's); plant 'to mature in shortening days' — a Maine fall crop, not a July one

bed30.note: two rows at 8 in; Johnny's: disturb the roots as little as possible or it bolts

crops.watch_for: BOLTING — triggered by heat, long days, and root disturbance at transplant (Johnny's); aphids; parsleyworm; clip any seed stalks that form (Johnny's)
crops.watering: Adequate, steady irrigation — water stress and heat push it straight to seed (Johnny's).
crops.method_notes: COOL-season ANNUAL — Johnny's is blunt: plant fennel 'to mature in shortening days with cooler temperatures, as high heat and long days encourage bolting.' In coastal Maine that means a midspring sowing for bulbs by late summer, or a summer sowing for fall bulbs. Bulbs tolerate light frost, so it is a legitimate September-October crop here. Transplant gently in 4-6 weeks or direct-sow; the bulb is swollen leaf bases, harvested when the base thickens (Johnny's). No strong companion claims — fennel is the herb most companion charts tell you to plant apart.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds Fino fennel (maturity from direct seeding; cool-season bolting guidance; 6 in spacing; 4-6 wk transplant; clip seed stalks); growingtaste.com & gardeningknowhow variety roundups (Zefa Fino ~65-80 d, short-season favorite); UMaine MHGN June 2025 (fennel among herbs drawing tiger swallowtails when allowed to flower).

crops.name: Sweet marjoram
crops.label: marjoram row

planting.note: 12 plants at 6-8 in (Johnny's); a small soft herb that tolerates crowding

bed30.note: three rows at 8 in; pinch growing tips to force branching (Johnny's)

crops.watch_for: root rot in soggy soil; aphids; wilts fast if the soil dries — Johnny's: it 'will not tolerate dry soils'
crops.watering: Moist, never dry, never soggy — the one Mediterranean herb that wants regular water.
crops.method_notes: TENDER PERENNIAL — Johnny's lists marjoram zones 9-11 and Fedco bluntly says 'grown as an annual in the North': in zone 5b plant it like a summer annual and don't expect it back. UMaine's Maine Home Garden News groups marjoram with the pollinator-friendly plants that 'don't survive our winters.' Start indoors 8-10 weeks (Johnny's); harvest whole plants just as flowering begins. Same genus as oregano but it is the soft, tender, winter-tender cousin.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Sweet marjoram 80-95 d; zones 9-11; 8-10 wk indoor start; 6-8 in spacing; drought note); Fedco (Origanum majorana 80-95 d, 'grown as an annual in the North'); UMaine MHGN June 2025 (marjoram among pollinator-friendly tender perennials).

crops.name: Chervil
crops.label: chervil strip

planting.note: two 8-ft rows sown shallow (light needed to germinate, Johnny's); also sow ~60 days before first frost for fall

bed30.note: three rows at 4 in — a tight, low, fast crop that wants cool weather

crops.watch_for: BOLTS fast in heat — Fedco: 'in warmer locations performs best as a fall crop'; slugs in wet springs; keep cut so it doesn't flower
crops.watering: Light but constant moisture (Fedco); it is a cool-weather plant that hates dry spells.
crops.method_notes: COOL-season ANNUAL and the classic French fine herbe, too delicate for drying. Slow-bolting strains (Fedco's) aside, treat it as early-spring and fall crop: Johnny's culture calls for direct sowing in early spring and again ~60 days before first frost. It self-sows if you let it. Chervil is standard in Eliot Coleman's winter-salad greenhouse mix in the Winter Harvest Handbook, and in the summer bed it is happier in the shade of taller crops (classic lettuce-bed partner).
crops.source: Fedco (Chervil 60 d to full maturity; harvest leaves 6-8 wk after sowing; fall-crop note; mesclun staple); Johnny's Selected Seeds (chervil culture: direct sow spring + 60 d before first frost; 6 in spacing; light needed to germinate); Eliot Coleman, The Winter Harvest Handbook (chervil as winter greenhouse salad crop).

crops.name: Calendula
crops.label: calendula edge

planting.note: 12 plants at 6-12 in (Johnny's); direct-sow or start 4-5 wk inside

bed30.note: three rows at 8 in, or use it as the bed's front edge — it flowers from June to hard frost

crops.watch_for: powdery mildew in humid late summer; aphids on buds; NOTE: UNH insectary research found calendula also hosted imported cabbageworm — keep it off the brassica beds if you can
crops.watering: Rich, well-drained soil (Johnny's); steady water, deadhead daily for continuous bloom.
crops.method_notes: COOL-season hardy ANNUAL — frost-tolerant, so it goes out early and flowers 'from summer to heavy frost' (Johnny's, which recommends 2-3 sowings 3 weeks apart for continuous bloom). UMaine's four-year bee study singles out 'pot marigold' as one of three direct-seeded annuals that flower long without deadheading and reseed themselves year after year — plant it once on the bed edge and it runs itself. Also a hoverfly flower in UMaine's June 2025 article; but see the UNH caveat about cabbageworm.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Flashback Mix 50-55 d; spacing 6-12 in; 2-3 successive sowings; flowers to heavy frost); UMaine Bulletin #2076 (pot marigold among top self-sowing direct-seeded bee annuals); UMaine MHGN June 2025 (calendula listed as pollinator-friendly annual); UNH insectary research report 2017-18 (calendula hosted imported cabbageworm).

crops.name: Chamomile (German)
crops.label: chamomile strip

planting.note: 12 plants at 8 in (Johnny's); press seeds onto the surface — light needed to germinate

bed30.note: three rows at 8 in; 15-24 in tall, airy, self-sows everywhere

crops.watch_for: aphids in the flower heads; pick flowers at full bloom and keep picking — Johnny's says 3-4 cuttings a season
crops.watering: Sandy, well-drained soil (Johnny's); water steadily while establishing, then let it be.
crops.method_notes: The garden tea chamomile is GERMAN chamomile (Matricaria recutita), a COOL-season hardy ANNUAL — 60-65 days to flower (Johnny's). Johnny's culture notes it 'self-sows readily. May become invasive, if allowed to do so' — in a kitchen-garden bed that is a feature: one planting becomes a permanent volunteer. (Roman chamomile, Chamaemelum nobile, is the hardy-groundcover perennial alternative.) Classic companion charts credit chamomile with improving onions (Burpee). Harvest timing only: gather flowers in full bloom.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Common Chamomile, Matricaria recutita, 60-65 d; 8 in spacing; light-needed germination; self-sows readily note; 3-4 cuttings); Burpee companion chart (chamomile improves onion growth and flavor).

crops.name: Borage
crops.label: borage station

planting.note: 4 plants at 12 in (Johnny's) — a taprooted 2-3 ft plant; DIRECT-SOW, transplants hate it (Johnny's)

bed30.note: two rows at 12 in; one or two plants near bee-pollinated crops does the pollinator job

crops.watch_for: aphids cluster on flower stems late summer; powdery mildew if crowded; everything else ignores it
crops.watering: Average soil, little water once up — it 'grows well even in poor soils' (Johnny's).
crops.method_notes: Hardy ANNUAL and the single best bee flower in UMaine's four-year study — common borage was among the most-visited plants of ~90 tested, and UMaine lists it as one of three direct-seeded annuals that reseed themselves year after year (Bulletin #2076). Plant one or two near the squash/cucumber rows for pollination, and let them set seed: they'll come back forever. Johnny's: direct-sow after soil warms, thin to 12 in, harvest flowers as it begins to bloom.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Borage 50-60 d; direct-sow, taproot, thin to 12 in; self-sows); UMaine Bulletin #2076 (common borage among most-visited bee plants; self-seeding annual); Park Seed borage profile (classic companion claims: heavier strawberry fruiting, cucumber/squash yields, tomato hornworm note — garden lore).

crops.name: Nasturtium
crops.label: nasturtium edge

planting.note: 8 plants at 8-12 in (Johnny's); direct-sow 1/2-1 in deep after frost — roots resent transplant

bed30.note: two rows, or better: one row along the bed's edge so trailing types spill onto the path

crops.watch_for: APHIDS — they swarm nasturtium by design (that's the trap crop working; Wisconsin/Penn State); flea beetles; cabbageworms; rich soil grows leaves with few flowers (Johnny's), so feed it nothing
crops.watering: Well-drained, not rich, not wet; once the black aphids arrive, rinse them off or let them feed the hoverflies.
crops.method_notes: Warm-season ANNUAL, frost-tender — the last flower out and the first to die. Its job in the Coleman-style bed is trap cropping: nasturtium's mustard-oil chemistry pulls aphids and cabbageworms off the brassicas and beans (Wisconsin Horticulture; Penn State's companion-planting piece) — but a trap crop only works as a monitored bait, so shake off or pinch out the aphid colonies before they explode and spill back. Everything — leaves, flowers, seed pods — is edible, but that is a harvest note, not a processing claim.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Nasturtium 55-65 d; direct-sow 1/2-1 in; 8-12 in spacing; low-fertility soil for blooms); Wisconsin Horticulture Extension nasturtium profile & Penn State Extension 'Herbs Make Good Plant Partners' (trap-crop mechanism); Burpee companion chart (nasturtium deters bean beetles).

crops.name: Echinacea
crops.label: echinacea corner

planting.note: 6 plants at 12-18 in; sow 8-10 wk inside or direct-sow in fall for natural stratification (Johnny's)

bed30.note: two rows at 12-18 in; give it the sunniest corner — it is a 3-4 ft statement plant

crops.watch_for: ASTER YELLOWS — vectored by the aster leafhopper; UMaine's IPM page lists coneflowers among its hosts and UMaine's own Echinacea trials screened plants against it (leafhopper exclusion); Japanese beetles chew petals in July; powdery mildew
crops.watering: Average, well-drained soil (Johnny's); drought-tolerant once established; water in the first summer only.
crops.method_notes: RELIABLY HARDIY perennial (Johnny's: zones 3-10). The 300-365 day figure is Johnny's days-from-seeding to first bloom — a plant that flowers in year two and lives for years, so in the planner it is an establishment crop: it needs ~90 frost-free days to get going, then it overwinters. UMaine's bee-pasture work for wild blueberry pollination included echinacea in its flower mixes, and UMaine research on organic Echinacea production is the local fact base for it. Plant it as the pollinator anchor of the perennial corner; it is a garden plant here, not a medicinal crop.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (E. purpurea 300-365 d from seeding; zones 3-10; 8-10 wk indoor start; fall direct-sow option; powwow-type hybrids 126-165 d); UMaine IPM aster leafhopper factsheet (coneflowers as aster-yellows hosts); UMaine Echinacea organic-production trials (aster yellows worse in open field — screened cages); UMaine bee-pasture fact sheet for lowbush blueberry (echinacea in seed mixes).

crops.name: Yarrow
crops.label: yarrow edge

planting.note: 6 plants at 12-24 in (Johnny's); sow 8-10 wk inside, direct-sow late spring/fall; divide every 3-4 yr

bed30.note: two rows at 12 in; flat flower heads are landing pads for hoverflies and parasitic wasps — keep it at the bed corners

crops.watch_for: powdery mildew in still, humid corners; aphids on stems; otherwise one of the toughest plants in the garden (zones 2-9, Johnny's: 'any well-drained soil')
crops.watering: None once established — Johnny's calls it 'any well-drained soil' and it laughs at drought.
crops.method_notes: RELIABLY HARDIY perennial (zones 2-9). This is the bed's insectary backbone: UConn's IPM lab insectary list documents common yarrow as a documented nectar and overwintering resource for hoverflies and parasitoid wasps — the same hoverflies whose larvae eat aphids (UMaine MHGN June 2025), and parasitoids that target brassica caterpillars and aphids. It blooms in the 120-130 day range from seed (Johnny's) and flowers all summer if cut; divide every 3-4 years to keep it vigorous (Johnny's).
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Yarrow 120-130 d; zones 2-9; 8-10 wk indoor start; divide every 3-4 yr); UConn IPM & Entomology Lab insectary-plants list (Achillea millefolium: nectar/overwintering for hoverflies, parasitoids); Fedco (yarrow: perennial zones 3-10, full sun, good drainage, rebloom if cut back); UMaine MHGN June 2025 (hoverfly biology/aphid predation).

crops.name: Bee balm
crops.label: bee-balm corner

planting.note: 4 plants at 12-18 in (Johnny's), stretched toward 24 in where mildew pressure is high (Iowa State)

bed30.note: two rows at 18 in — and Iowa State says 2-2.5 ft apart, full sun, divided every 2-3 yr, or powdery mildew owns it by August

crops.watch_for: POWDERY MILDEW — the defining complaint of the genus (Iowa State: worst on crowded plants and part shade; pick resistant cvs like Jacob Cline, Marshall's Delight, Raspberry Wine); rust in wet seasons
crops.watering: Evenly moist soil likes it (it's a streambank plant), but water the soil, never overhead.
crops.method_notes: RELIABLY HARDIY perennial (Johnny's: zones 4-10). From seed it 'does not usually flower until the second year' (Johnny's) — divisions flower the first year, so buy or split. This is the hummingbird and bee magnet of the perennial corner — UMaine's bee research names common beebalm among the red flowers with UV markings that bees read as more than red (Bulletin #2076) — making it real pollination support for the squash and cucumber rows. One rule governs where it goes: full sun, wide spacing, and division every 2-3 years, or mildew takes it.
crops.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (Monarda: 6-8 wk indoor start; 12-18 in spacing; zones 4-10; flowers second year; divide mature plants); Iowa State University Extension (bee balm powdery mildew: full sun, space 2-2.5 ft, divide every 2-3 yr, resistant cultivars); UMaine Bulletin #2076 (common beebalm, red flowers with UV markings).

crops.name: Pole bean
crops.label: bean trellis

planting.note: one 8 ft row up a 6–8 ft trellis panel or net at the north edge of the bed, one plant per 6 in

bed30.note: single row against a trellis panel set at the north edge; Fedco sows 3–4 in apart along fencing, UMaine's wide-row hills run 24 in — 6 in is the bed middle ground

crops.watch_for: Mexican bean beetle (defoliates; UMaine), halo blight / bean mosaic / rust in a wet year (choose resistant varieties per UMaine #2190), and skimpy germination from sowing into cold wet soil — wait for 60°F ground
crops.watering: Even moisture from flowering to pod set; a dry spell then drops blossoms and turns pods stringy.
crops.method_notes: Coleman runs his rotation on legumes — beans and peas fix the nitrogen the heavy feeders spend — and trellises the vining ones so the bed face stays in full sun. Grow pole beans up a 6–8 ft panel at the bed's north edge (Fedco: fencing, plants 3–4 in apart), succession-sow every 2–3 weeks so flushes bridge instead of glutting (UMaine), and pick every few days: a plant left with mature pods stops producing. Inoculate with bean/pea Rhizobium the first time a bed grows beans (Fedco/UMaine).
crops.source: UMaine Cooperative Extension planting chart (pole beans 5/15–6/15 central ME, 24-in hills, ~12 lbs/10 ft); UMaine Bulletin #2190 (pole varieties: Blue Lake strains, Fortex, Kentucky Blue, Scarlet Runner); UMaine Bulletin #4311 (Mexican bean beetle, 3-week succession plantings); Fedco pole bean culture (6–8 ft fencing, 3–4 in apart, inoculate); Johnny's Fortex (60 days, trellis required) and Johnny's pole-bean video (55–65 days typical); Eliot Coleman, The New Organic Grower (3rd ed.) — 30-in bed/12-in path system, trellised legumes in rotation.

crops.name: Snow pea
crops.label: pea trellis

planting.note: two 8 ft rows up a trellis at the north edge of the bed, seeds 2 in apart

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart, both climbing a trellis/net at the north edge; UMaine sows peas 1–2 in apart in rows 18–36 in apart — the bed version tightens row spacing

crops.watch_for: Pea aphid spreading pea enation mosaic virus (yellowed, stunted, crinkled plants — the single worst pea disease), powdery mildew in a humid June (pick mildew-resistant types like Oregon Sugar Pod II), birds pulling seedlings — net or row-cover
crops.watering: Even moisture at flowering; wet feet rot the vines off in a cool spring, so don't overwater.
crops.method_notes: The earliest real harvest of the year — sow as soon as the soil can be worked (UMaine: 4/15+ in central ME, 10–14 days earlier on the coast). Trellis from sowing day: Coleman's Four-Season Harvest design (posts plus netting) keeps 38-in vines upright, doubles the yield per bed foot and makes picking easy. Harvest flat, before the seeds swell — overmature peas turn starchy and stop the plant. Follow with a warm-season crop, or sow again for fall (MOFGA: August 1) under a row cover.
crops.source: UMaine Cooperative Extension planting chart (peas 1–2 in apart, 4/15–7/15 central ME; coastal 10–14 days earlier); UMaine Bulletin #4256 (snow peas as edible-pod type); UMaine pea-fall-crop answer (MOFGA Aug 1 fall sowing; see UMaine Bulletin #2752 on season extension); Johnny's Oregon Sugar Pod II (60 days, 38-in vines, mildew/PEMV-resistant class); Eliot Coleman, Four-Season Harvest (pea trellis design).

crops.name: Fava bean
crops.label: fava rows

planting.note: two 8 ft rows across the bed, one plant per 6 in; sturdy stems need no support

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart; MOFGA sows 6–8 in apart in drills at least 12 in apart (2–3 rows per 4.5 ft bed), Fedco sows 3–4 in apart

crops.watch_for: Black bean aphid (Aphis fabae) colonies on growing tips in cool damp springs — pinch infested tips; chocolate spot (Botrytis fabae) in humid spells — space for airflow, don't overhead-water; rust (Uromyces viciae-fabae) by July
crops.watering: Steady moisture through flowering and pod set — favas are 'sensitive to heat and drought at flowering' (Fedco OGS) and will drop pods.
crops.method_notes: The fertility engine before the heat: favas fix nitrogen in cool soil when Phaseolus beans can't even germinate, and they thrive 40–60°F (MOFGA). Sow 'as early as peas' (Fedco) — soil just thawed, mid-to-late April on the midcoast. Whole plants (small-seeded 'bell bean' favas) can be turned in at flowering as a frost-hardy green manure — Coleman's rotation leans on exactly this legume-to-heavy-feeder turnover. In Maine fall-sown favas winterkill at 10–15°F (Fedco OGS), so treat this as an early-spring crop, not an overwintered one. Pick at green-shell stage; beans you can't squeeze out of the membrane are over-the-hill. In midcoast zone 5b/6a, sow in April and harvest before the July heat (MOFGA harvest timing: after asparagus, before shell peas).
crops.source: MOFGA 'Fava Beans' (sow as soil thaws, 6–8 in apart, drills ≥12 in apart, 2–3 rows per 4.5 ft bed, thrice 40–60°F; Bonsall/Thorkildsen bed-edge greens); Fedco Windsor Fava (sow 3–4 in apart 'as early as peas', green-shell harvest; veggie chart: 'ASAP, min germination 40°'); Fedco Organic Growers Supply Bell Beans (frost-hardy winter annual; winterkills at 10–15°F; drops blossoms over 70°F — spring crop in ME); AHDB field-bean guide & field-bean IPM review (black bean aphid, chocolate spot Botrytis fabae, rust Uromyces viciae-fabae); Eliot Coleman, The New Organic Grower (3rd ed.) — legumes as the rotation's fertility engine.

crops.name: Edamame
crops.label: edamame block

planting.note: two 8 ft rows, one plant per 6 in; compact 2 ft bushes need no support, single main sowing for coastal Maine

bed30.note: two rows 12–15 in apart; UMaine/Mid-Atlantic field spacing is 2–4 in within 30–36 in rows — 6 in suits a bed

crops.watch_for: Soybean aphid late in the season (UMD/Mid-Atlantic thresholds: 250 per plant through pod set), deer browsing the row, and seed rot from sowing into cold wet soil — wait for 60°F ground
crops.watering: Even moisture from bloom to pod fill; a dry spell at pod set cuts seeds per pod.
crops.method_notes: A warm-soil legume: direct-sow after frost when the soil hits 60°F — late May on the midcoast — or seed rots (UMD; getgrowli/Maine tables agree). Inoculate with soybean Bradyrhizobium the first year in ground new to soybeans (UMD). Fedco's Chiba (83 days) is the Maine-reliable pick; Shirofumi and Tankuro run 90–91. The flush is concentrated and the harvest window at green-pod stage is only days before beans harden, so one main sowing beats succession here. MOFGA's Will Bonsall plants edamame among the sweet corn to double row-foot yield — a good use of the bed edge. Pick when pods are plump and bright green.
crops.source: Fedco edamame (Chiba 83 d, Shirofumi 91 d, Tankuro 90 d; sow after frost); UMD Extension / Mid-Atlantic Commercial Veg Recommendations edamame factsheet (varieties 75–87 d incl. Midori Giant 75, Chiba Green 82; rows 30–36 in, seeds 2–4 in apart ≤1/2 in deep; inoculate Bradyrhizobium; soybean aphid threshold); MOFGA 'Grow Edamame' (Bonsall interplants with sweet corn); UMaine Grains, Pulses & Oilseeds soybean notes.

crops.name: Popcorn
crops.label: popcorn block

planting.note: a block, not a row — a 4x8 holds four short rows of six; better still, three adjacent beds or a corner of the garden

bed30.note: corn is wind-pollinated and needs a block — three or more adjacent 30 in beds minimum, or grow it as a patch elsewhere; within a bed, two rows 12 in apart at 6–8 in (Johnny's: 6–7 in, blocks of ≥4 rows)

crops.watch_for: Corn earworm at silk, raccoons the night it's ready, and a wet cool fall that stalls dry-down — in coastal Maine pick varieties that finish under 110 days including drying (UMaine)
crops.watering: Heavy drinker from tassel through grain fill; drought then means poor fill and weak popping.
crops.method_notes: Corn is wind-pollinated: grow it in a block (Johnny's: at least 4 rows) or the ears are all chaff. UMaine's Maine-specific rule for popcorn: choose varieties that mature in under 110 days including drying down to ~20% kernel moisture (Strawberry, Cherry Berry, Perdue 410, Gourmet Mushroom, Top Pop, Dakota Black), because wet falls stall the cure. Let ears dry on the stalk until husks rattle, finish curing under cover, and test-pop before storing (Johnny's: ideal 13–14.5% moisture). Heavy nitrogen feeder — plant it behind a legume bed in the rotation.
crops.source: UMaine Extension Ask-the-Expert 'What is the best type of popcorn to grow in Maine?' (varieties <110 days incl. dry-down to ~20% moisture; 'very thirsty'); Johnny's dry/ornamental corn growing info (sow ¾–1 in deep, 6–7 in apart, blocks of ≥4 rows for pollination; harvest hard glossy kernels, cure to 13–14.5% moisture, test-pop); Fedco corn culture (min soil 55–60°F, frost-tender, heavy N); Sand Hill Preservation popcorn catalog (varieties 80–125 days); Cornell/Wisconsin popcorn notes (maturity before frost = popping quality).

crops.name: Sunflower
crops.label: seed heads

planting.note: one row down the middle of the bed, six plants at 18 in — confection types want room for one big head each

bed30.note: single row down the middle; 18 in between plants for large seed heads (UMaine oilseed rate ≈30,000/ac; tall seed types like Mammoth prefer 18–24 in)

crops.watch_for: Birds (goldfinches and friends) strip ripe heads — bag them as they mature; deer eat the foliage (UMaine); downy mildew in a wet year — choose resistant types
crops.watering: Deep weekly soak while the head forms; moisture stress at bloom cuts seed set.
crops.method_notes: Direct-sow after the last frost, or start 2–3 weeks inside (UMaine). For edible seed grow confection types (Mammoth Grey Stripe, Russian Mammoth — 90–110 days), not pollenless cut-flower hybrids. Succession-plant a couple of sowings 2–3 weeks apart to stretch the harvest (UMaine). Seed is ready when the head back turns lemon-yellow and the seeds show black-and-white striping (K-State), roughly 30–45 days after petals drop — cut, dry, then thresh. Fedco says Will Bonsall grows pole beans up sunflower stalks: give the sunflowers a two-week head start, about 2 bean seeds per stalk. Beyond its own harvest it is the garden's best bee pasture.
crops.source: UMaine Extension Q&A 'Growing sunflowers' (direct seed after last frost or start 2–3 wks inside; 50–95 d to maturity per packet; succession plantings late June–mid July; deer love them); UMaine SARE oilseed sunflower profile (May planting, ~30,000 seeds/ac); Fedco pole-bean culture (Bonsall: pole beans on sunflower stalks, 2-week head start, 2 seeds per stalk); Univ. of Minnesota Extension (70–120 d to bloom; most mature 85–95 d; mammoth types to 110+); Kansas State (maturity cues: lemon-yellow head back, black-and-white striped seed); trade/ext seed guides (Russian Mammoth ~105 d).

crops.name: Asparagus
crops.label: asparagus bed

planting.note: five crowns per person is the UMaine rule of thumb; a 4x8 bed holds two rows of seven 1-ft-apart crowns

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart in a 30 in bed; UMaine wants 5 ft between commercial rows, but a bed only works if you accept denser, shorter-lived planting

crops.watch_for: asparagus beetle and spotted asparagus beetle chewing spear tips, Fusarium crown rot on wet low-pH soil, asparagus rust on damp ferns
crops.watering: One inch a week for the first three years to build the bed; established plants need water only in serious drought (UMaine).
crops.method_notes: The classic permanent bed — Coleman treats it as the anchor of the perennial corner, established once and then out of the rotation for 15-20 years (The New Organic Grower). Prepare soil to 10-12 in deep and lime to 6.5-7.0 pH a season before planting; a poor bed can't be fixed later. Plant one-year-old crowns (healthy roots are white inside, not reddish-brown) after soil warms past 50F. Year-one discipline is total: no harvest at all; year two harvest two weeks, year three three weeks, year four four, and stop by June 15 in Maine so ferns rebuild the crown. Male hybrids (Jersey Knight, Jersey Supreme, Jersey Giant) out-yield and outlive the old open-pollinated types. Do not plant where asparagus has grown before.
crops.source: UMaine Bulletin #2071 Growing Asparagus in Maine; Eliot Coleman, The New Organic Grower (3rd ed.), perennial crops chapter.

permanent.note: Needs a deep, well-drained, weed-free site prepared a year ahead; lime to 6.5-7.0 pH before planting. It is a permanent, once-planted bed occupying ground for 15-20 years, so it never rotates through the vegetable beds.

crops.name: Rhubarb
crops.label: rhubarb crowns

planting.note: two crowns fill a 4x8 bed; UMaine spacing is 3-4 ft each way, 5 ft for the big varieties

bed30.note: one crown every 3-4 ft; a single mature crown exceeds 4 ft across, so a whole 30 in bed holds one plant comfortably

crops.watch_for: crown rot in wet heavy soil, leaf fungal spots in cool damp weather, rhubarb curculio in weedy plantings
crops.watering: Drought tolerant once established; in hot dry spells soak to 3-6 in deep (roots feed at 12-18 in, so water hard, not often).
crops.method_notes: A cool-climate crop that needs our cold winters to go dormant — no Maine chill problem at all. Best started as a divided crown with 1-2 eyes and at least a 2-in cross-section of storage root; seed gives variable plants. Do NOT harvest any stalks in year one; harvest from year two on, never more than half the stalks, and stop by about August 31 so the crown rebuilds for winter. Remove flower stalks as they form. Dig, split and replant the crown every four to five years to keep stalks thick. Leaves are oxalic-acid toxic; stalks only.
crops.source: UMaine Bulletin #2514 Growing Rhubarb in Maine; Eliot Coleman, The New Organic Grower (3rd ed.), perennial crops chapter.

permanent.note: Well-drained loam, full sun, generous spacing (3-4 ft) — a crown rewards space and forgives most soils. It occupies its corner for a decade or more and gets split every 4-5 years, so it never rotates through the annual beds.

crops.name: Jerusalem artichoke (sunchoke)
crops.label: sunchoke hedge

planting.note: plant pieces 4 in deep, 12-14 in apart along a row — feed the hedge at the back of the garden

bed30.note: one row, tubers 12-14 in apart; this is a tall hedge plant, not a bed occupant

crops.watch_for: few pests; the persistence is the pest — missed tubers resprout, so plant where it can spread; white mold in wet years
crops.watering: Soak at planting, then mostly none — established plants shrug off drought and produce in poor soil.
crops.method_notes: Native sunflower relative, hardy as Maine gets. Plant tubers 3-4 in deep in early spring after frost; a pound of seed tubers makes an 18-20 ft row. It grows a 6-8 ft flowering hedge by fall — treat it as a productive screen, not a bed crop. Harvest after a couple of frosts sweetens the tubers; dig what you need, leave the rest in the ground (they store perfectly in situ) and re-plant a few small tubers each spring, or it will wander. Once in, it is nearly impossible to eradicate, so site it deliberately. Coleman lists it among the winter-harvestable perennials (Four-Season Harvest).
crops.source: Fedco sunchoke growing notes and Johnny's Selected Seeds Jerusalem artichoke key growing information; Eliot Coleman, Four-Season Harvest, winter crops chapter.

permanent.note: Grows almost anywhere but prefers light sandy soil; full sun for best tuber bulk. It is a self-perpetuating, spreading perennial that never leaves the garden once planted — a deliberate permanent hedge, not a rotation crop.

crops.name: Sea kale
crops.label: sea kale crowns

planting.note: eight crowns at 18-24 in spacing fill a 4x8 bed of its own

bed30.note: one row, 18-24 in apart; plants form a 1-3 ft rosette with 3 ft flower racemes

crops.watch_for: flea beetles on young growth (it is a brassica), slugs in wet springs; deer will graze the young leaves
crops.watering: Water well through the first season; once established it is a tough coastal perennial that takes dry spells and salt wind.
crops.method_notes: The old English asparagus-substitute: a zone-5 hardy perennial brassica from the seashore. Start from root cuttings taken in winter (easier and truer than seed), or scarified seed started indoors like broccoli. Let it settle in year one — harvest begins the second year and improves after. The Victorian trick Coleman describes in Four-Season Harvest is forcing: cover crowns with an opaque pot or bucket in early spring and the blanched, pale shoots are the delicacy — cut at 3-10 in before they green. Leave the plants to leaf out after forcing so they rebuild for next year. Best in sharp-draining, even slightly chalky soil; part shade is fine, unlike asparagus.
crops.source: Fedco Sea Kale Perennial Greens listing (hardiness, culture, forcing); Royal Horticultural Society Crambe maritima plant page; Eliot Coleman, Four-Season Harvest.

permanent.note: A true perennial vegetable occupying permanent ground for a decade. Sharp-draining, sandy or chalky soil, full sun to part shade; thrives near coast. Never rotated — a permanent crown planting harvested for its forced spring shoots.

crops.name: Strawberry
crops.label: strawberry matted row

planting.note: ten plants per 4x8 matted row at 18 in spacing; 100 plants feeds a family of four with surplus

bed30.note: one matted row, plants 18 in apart, row held to 24 in wide with runners pinned back

crops.watch_for: gray mold (Botrytis) in wet June weather, tarnished plant bug and strawberry bud weevil distorting fruit, red stele and Verticillium root rots — buy resistant varieties and move sites
crops.watering: One to two inches a week through fruit set; soaker the rows, not overhead, to keep gray mold down.
crops.method_notes: Technically perennial, practically a 3-5 year bed — plan to replant on fresh ground (never where tomatoes/peppers/eggplant grew: Verticillium). June-bearers: plant early spring, pinch ALL flowers the first year so runners fill an 18-in-apart matted row, mulch with 6-8 in of straw in mid-November and pull it off in spring. Earliglow, Wendy, Cavendish, Flavorfest and Jewel are the UMaine-tested performers. A fall/winter planting of day-neutrals (Seascape, Albion, Tribute, Tristar) can be grown as an annual for later fruit. Beds decline hard after year three — rotating through new ground is the honest plan.
crops.source: UMaine Bulletin #2067 Growing Strawberries (site, spacing, varieties, renovation).

permanent.note: A short-lived perennial that must rotate: plant on new ground every 3-5 years to dodge soil-borne root rots. Full sun, sandy loam, 18-in matted rows. Not a permanent bed in the asparagus sense — it is a renewable perennial.

crops.name: Blackberry
crops.label: blackberry hills

planting.note: hill system: two plants per 4x8 at 4 ft apart, rows 8-12 ft

bed30.note: not a bed crop — hill system at 4 ft, rows 8-12 ft, trellised; canes grow 4-6 ft

crops.watch_for: spotted wing drosophila on ripe fruit (pick daily, chill immediately), cane borers, viruses — plant certified virus-free stock and destroy wild brambles within 600 ft
crops.watering: One to two inches a week in the season; drought during ripening makes hard, small berries.
crops.method_notes: Hardiness is the honest catch: UMaine says blackberries lack the hardiness for anywhere but well-sheltered southern Maine sites — temps below 5F injure or kill the canes, so Wiscasset is the right edge of the map (coastal shelter helps). Plant dormant one-year canes in spring, hill system at 4 ft; trellis or they flop. Thorny Darrow and Illini are the varieties UMaine lists; thornless types need even milder sites. Fruit comes on second-year canes: pinch new canes at 4 ft to force fruiting laterals, then cut out every cane that fruited, right after harvest. Netting for birds, and pick daily in the SWD window.
crops.source: UMaine Bulletin #2066 Growing Raspberries and Blackberries (hardiness limits, hill spacing, pruning); Bulletin #2172 Raspberry and Blackberry Varieties for Maine (Darrow, Illini).

permanent.note: Perennial roots, biennial canes — each cane fruits once then dies, so it lives as a managed hedgerow with a trellis, outside the rotation. Full sun, well-drained sandy loam. Marginal hardiness in zone 5b: plant only in a sheltered, south-facing site.

crops.name: Highbush blueberry
crops.label: highbush blueberry bushes

planting.note: one bush per 4x8 — this is an orchard/hedge plant at 5-7 ft spacing, not a bed crop

bed30.note: 5-7 ft between plants, 8-10 ft between rows; netted against birds when fruit colors

crops.watch_for: blueberry maggot in ripe fruit, mummy berry shriveling berries in wet springs, birds (netting is the only effective control)
crops.watering: One to two inches a week; shallow roots — a 4-6 in mulch layer of pine needles or wood chips is the best watering tool.
crops.method_notes: Soil is everything: highbush blueberry needs pH 4.5-5.2 and won't wait while you amend later — test and acidify with sulfur well before planting. Plant 2-3 year nursery bushes in early spring at 5-7 ft; two or more varieties improve set and spread the season (Patriot, Northland, Bluecrop, Blueray are UMaine's northern picks). Year-one and -two discipline: pick off all flower clusters both years, tolerate a small crop in year three, full crop at four to five. Prune dormant, January-March: canes older than six years come out. Protect below -25F is the real zone limit — Wiscasset coastal is fine.
crops.source: UMaine Bulletin #2253 Growing Highbush Blueberries (pH, spacing, varieties, pruning, pests).

permanent.note: Demands acid, well-drained sandy loam rich in organic matter — a dedicated ericaceous bed, kept separate from lime-loving vegetables. A 20-30 year permanent shrub planting, renewed by cane pruning, never rotated.

crops.name: Lowbush blueberry (wild blueberry)
crops.label: wild blueberry patch

planting.note: 1 ft x 1 ft sod blocks, set 1-2 ft apart; one block per 4x8, or sod a dedicated patch

bed30.note: two rows, plants/sod 1-2 ft apart; they spread into a ground-cover patch

crops.watch_for: blueberry maggot and mummy berry (same as highbush), woody weed competition — cut saplings and ferns three times a year; birds at ripeness
crops.watering: About one inch a week, spread over the week, for the first two establishment years and in dry crop years; extra water invites disease.
crops.method_notes: Maine's native crop — the state's blueberry program is built on it. Wild blueberries want acidic pH 4.0-4.5, sandy well-drained soil, and full sun; they will NOT grow in a vegetable bed, so give them their own patch. Easiest route is transplanting sod (1 ft blocks) from a reputable nursery, or buy plants 1-2 ft apart. Pinch off ALL blossoms the first two years so roots establish — the single most important discipline. Then manage on a two-year mow cycle: mow half the patch to 1.5 in every fall, alternate sides yearly, and you get berries every year. About half a pound per square foot once established (year four).
crops.source: UMaine Bulletin #2073 Growing Wild Blueberries at Home (soil, pH, sod, mowing cycle, water); UMaine Home Garden Lowbush Blueberry Planting Guide.

permanent.note: Native to Maine's acid, sandy, well-drained coastal soils — replicate those conditions or it fails. A permanent ground-cover patch (1-2 ft tall) managed on a biennial mowing cycle, entirely outside the vegetable rotation.

crops.name: Red currant
crops.label: red currant bushes

planting.note: two bushes per 4x8 at 3-5 ft spacing; rows 8-10 ft

bed30.note: one row, plants 3-5 ft apart — currants tolerate more shade than most fruit

crops.watch_for: currant aphids curling new leaves, powdery mildew, anthracnose leaf spot in wet years, currant borer tunneling canes; white pine blister rust is the regulatory pest
crops.watering: Keep the root zone cool and moist — 2-3 in of mulch does most of the work; this is not a drought-tolerant bush.
crops.method_notes: IMPORTANT — LEGAL FIRST: Maine quarantines all Ribes (currants and gooseberries) to protect white pine from blister rust, and Wiscasset is in Lincoln County, one of the fully prohibited counties on the Maine Forest Service quarantine list. Sale, transport, further planting and possession are prohibited. If any pine is nearby, plant something else. Where legal (check your county): currants are the easiest berries in the Northeast, fruiting in June on 2-3 year wood. Plant 1-2 year stock in early fall or very early spring, remove all first-year flowers, expect a light crop year two and full crop year three. Prune dormant, keeping about 6-8 bearing canes by renewal — older wood fruits poorly. Rovada is a reliable red; they prefer pH about 6.5 and tolerate part shade.
crops.source: Cornell Fruit Resources: Gooseberries and Currants (site, spacing, pruning, pests); Maine Forest Service white pine blister rust quarantine via UMaine Extension Ask the Expert 2024.

permanent.note: Cool, moist, well-drained soil with organic matter; tolerates partial shade. A permanent shrub maintained by cane renewal pruning. LEGAL CHECK REQUIRED: Ribes are under quarantine in Lincoln County, Maine (white pine blister rust) — do not plant without confirming current county status.

crops.name: Black currant
crops.label: black currant bushes

planting.note: two bushes per 4x8 at 3-5 ft spacing; rows 8-10 ft

bed30.note: one row, plants 3-5 ft apart

crops.watch_for: currant aphids, powdery mildew, leaf spot; black currants are the most susceptible Ribes to white pine blister rust — the quarantine pest
crops.watering: Keep the root zone cool and moist with mulch; consistent water through fruit swell in early summer.
crops.method_notes: Same Maine legal warning as red currant — Ribes quarantine covers black currants in Lincoln County (Wiscasset); check the Maine Forest Service map before planning anything. Note the historical federal ban targeted black currants specifically as the most rust-susceptible. Where legal, the resistant cultivars (Consort, Crusader, Titania — bred immune or resistant to blister rust) are the only sensible choice in the Northeast. Culture mirrors red currant: 3-5 ft spacing, remove first-year flowers, full crop by year three, dormant renewal pruning of canes older than three years. Fruit is much higher in vitamin C than red currants and makes the classic currant jelly.
crops.source: Cornell Fruit Resources: Gooseberries and Currants (cultivars, culture, pruning); UMaine Extension Ask the Expert on the Maine Ribes quarantine.

permanent.note: Cool, moist, well-drained soil, part shade OK. Use only blister-rust resistant cultivars where legal. LEGAL CHECK REQUIRED: black currants are the most rust-susceptible Ribes and are under quarantine in Lincoln County, Maine.

crops.name: Gooseberry
crops.label: gooseberry bushes

planting.note: two bushes per 4x8 at 3-5 ft spacing; rows 8-10 ft

bed30.note: one row, plants 3-5 ft apart; goosberries can be trellised to add airflow and ease picking

crops.watch_for: powdery mildew (the big one on European types — pick American cultivars), currant aphids, gooseberry fruitworm webbing berries, San Jose scale on old wood
crops.watering: Mulch and keep cool and moist; gooseberries suffer in hot dry sites, so a north-side or lightly shaded spot beats full sun here.
crops.method_notes: Legal warning identical to the currants — gooseberries are Ribes and fall under the same Maine quarantine covering Lincoln County (Wiscasset); verify county status before planting. Where legal, the American types (Poorman, Oregon Champion, Pixwell, Hinnonmaki Red/Yellow, Captivator) are the healthier, mildew-resistant choice in the East — European cultivars have the big fruit and the worst mildew. Culture like currants: remove first-year flowers, light crop year two, full by year three. Fruiting is on 2-3 year wood, so use the renewal-pruning pattern (about 8 bearing canes). Trellising the bushes improves air flow and harvest. Berries ripen over two weeks in late June; pick when colored.
crops.source: Cornell Fruit Resources: Gooseberries and Currants (American vs European types, spacing, mildew, pruning); UMaine Extension on the Maine Ribes quarantine.

permanent.note: Cool, moist, well-drained soil; prefers light shade in the Northeast, which makes it genuinely different from the full-sun berries. Permanent shrub maintained by renewal pruning. LEGAL CHECK REQUIRED: under Ribes quarantine in Lincoln County, Maine.

crops.name: Elderberry
crops.label: elderberry hedgerow

planting.note: one plant per 4x8 — this is a hedgerow shrub at 6-10 ft spacing, not a bed crop

bed30.note: shrubs 6-10 ft apart; they sucker into a hedgerow and shade everything within reach

crops.watch_for: powdery mildew in humid spells, cane borers in old canes, birds on the clusters; virtually pest-free otherwise
crops.watering: Keep well watered the entire first season — roots are shallow and the plants dry out fast; then only in real drought.
crops.method_notes: The most reliable 'native orchard' berry in Maine: hardy to zone 3, flowers late June so spring frosts almost never hit it. Nearly self-unfruitful, so plant two different cultivars within 60 ft (Adams 1 & 2, York, Johns, Nova are proven; UMaine runs elderberry workshops exactly because it thrives here). Shallow-rooted — never cultivate deeper than 2 in, hand-pull weeds, mulch. Canes fruit on the current season's growth, especially on second-year laterals, so the pruning rule is simple: in late winter remove all canes older than three years and keep one-, two- and three-year canes in balance. Harvest whole clusters late August-early September; uncooked berries are astringent and inedible. Cook before use. Grows in far wetter ground than most fruit, but not standing water.
crops.source: Cornell Cooperative Extension, Elderberries (gardening.cals.cornell.edu fruit factsheet): culture, spacing, pruning, harvest; UMaine Extension small-fruit programming.

permanent.note: Moist, fertile, well-drained soil, pH 5.5-6.5, full sun to part shade; tolerant of wetter ground than most berries. A suckering hedgerow shrub that must have room — not a bed crop. Renewed by cutting out canes older than three years.

crops.name: Honeyberry (haskap)
crops.label: honeyberry row

planting.note: two bushes per 4x8 at 3-4 ft in-row; rows 6-10 ft

bed30.note: one row, plants 3-4 ft apart; bushes reach 4-6 ft tall and wide

crops.watch_for: birds (net late May-early June — they find it first, it is the earliest fruit here), powdery mildew on susceptible cultivars, sunscald on exposed fruit
crops.watering: Not drought tolerant — moist, never soggy; drip is ideal. Deep water every 5-7 days in the high-summer stretch.
crops.method_notes: A genuinely cold-climate berry (native down to zone 2 plains and Scandinavian/Alaskan coasts) that thrives in Maine winters but needs two cultivars that bloom together for cross-pollination — most nurseries sell compatible pairs. Extremely early: ripens early to mid June, before strawberries, and the flowers take frost to about 19F, so springs here rarely cost the crop. Site in full sun with well-drained soil; pH is broadly adaptable. Light harvest begins year 3-4, mature bushes give 5-15 lb. Tundra, Borealis, Indigo Gem and Blue Lightning are the well-documented cultivars. Prune lightly in late winter — no more than a quarter of the bush — thinning oldest branches for air.
crops.source: Utah State University Extension, Haskap in the Garden (peer-reviewed; culture, spacing, cultivars, frost tolerance); Fedco/Johnny's haskap listings for New England availability.

permanent.note: Long-lived shrub (to 30 years), broadly pH-adaptable, needs moist well-drained soil and a second cultivar for pollination. Earliest-ripening berry in a Maine garden — a permanent planting that no annual bed can substitute for.

crops.name: Apple
crops.label: apple trees

planting.note: not a bed crop — dwarf trees at 6-8 ft spacing, semi-dwarf at 15 ft in cold regions

bed30.note: semi-dwarf 15 ft, dwarf 6-8 ft, standard 25 ft; cold-region spacing per UMaine

crops.watch_for: apple scab in our wet springs (plant resistant varieties), cedar-apple rust where junipers grow nearby, apple maggot and codling moth in the fruit, deer and voles on young trees
crops.watering: Five gallons a week per young tree in any week with under an inch of rain, through the first few growing seasons.
crops.method_notes: The most winter-hardy tree fruit and the one Maine does best — most varieties are at home here; the coastal 5b/6a site is prime apple country. Plant bare-root in April/early May (fall planting is wrong for New England), graft union 2-3 in above ground, stake dwarf trees, never fertilize the planting hole. Train to central leader, head whips to 30-36 in. Most varieties need a second, compatible variety for pollination — plant two that bloom together. Scab is the disease that decides everything in a wet climate: choose resistant varieties (Liberty, Enterprise, Freedom, Pristine, CrimsonCrisp per UMaine) or spray from green tip. Dwarf on M.9/M.26 yields in year 3-4; be honest that standard trees take 6-8. Pick a mix that ripens from August into October.
crops.source: UMaine Cooperative Extension, Growing Fruit Trees in Maine: Types of Fruit Trees, Spacing Trees in an Orchard, Bulletin #2411 Planting and Early Care of Fruit Trees.

permanent.note: Full sun, well-drained soil, at least 6 hours direct light; semi-dwarf at 15 ft spacing, dwarf at 6-8 ft. A permanent orchard tree producing for decades — entirely outside the vegetable rotation, with pollination, scab and deer management built in for the life of the tree.

crops.name: Pear (European)
crops.label: pear trees

planting.note: not a bed crop — pears are the largest tree fruit, give them the extra 5 ft beyond apple spacing

bed30.note: semi-dwarf pears about 20 ft, standards 30 ft — pears need an additional 5 ft over apples (UMaine)

crops.watch_for: fire blight (the defining pear disease in the East — plant resistant varieties), pear psylla, codling moth; deer browse young trees
crops.watering: Same as apple: five gallons a week while young whenever rain is under an inch; mature trees mostly fend for themselves.
crops.method_notes: Pears are hardier than their reputation — the cold-hardy European varieties are rated for zone 4 and do fine in coastal Maine. The honest catches: they are the slowest of the tree fruits to bear (commonly 5-7 years even on dwarfing stock — plan for it), and fire blight decides the variety list: plant resistant types (Harrow Delight, Magness, Maxine, Potomac, Seckel per UMaine; Blake's Pride for market quality). They also grow large: give them the extra 5 ft beyond apple spacing. Two compatible varieties needed for pollination. Central-leader training, keep the crotch angles wide (45-60 deg) — narrow crotches split with a heavy crop. Asian pears are zone 5 but dislike Maine's winter temperature swings, so European types are the honest recommendation for Wiscasset.
crops.source: UMaine Cooperative Extension, Types of Fruit Trees (pear varieties and hardiness), Spacing Trees in an Orchard.

permanent.note: Full sun, well-drained soil; the largest of the hardy tree fruits, needing generous spacing (20 ft semi-dwarf, 30 ft standard). Slow to come into bearing (5-7 years) but very long-lived. Permanent orchard tree outside the rotation.

crops.name: Plum (hybrid/European)
crops.label: plum trees

planting.note: not a bed crop — one tree per 4x8 plus orchard space; 10-18 ft between trees by rootstock

bed30.note: Myrobalan rootstock: 15-18 ft vigorous varieties, 12-15 ft low vigor (UMaine)

crops.watch_for: black knot on branches (the plum disease — prune out galls), plum curculio scarring fruit, rain splitting on Shiro/Methley/Superior, frost on the early bloom (plums flower a week before apples)
companions: another plum of the same type
crops.watering: Water young trees weekly in dry spells (2-5 gal); mature trees want no wet feet — well-drained site decides success.
crops.method_notes: Plums do well in Maine, with one calendar warning: they bloom about a week before apples, so a late frost can take the crop — plant on a slope with good air drainage, not in a frost pocket. Two pollination rules that matter: Japanese plums must be planted with other Japanese-type varieties (they will not pollinate from Europeans and vice versa), and Europeans (Stanley, Italian) are the hardier, more reliable choice for zone 5b. UMaine's hardy standouts include Toka, Superior, Alderman, Black Ice, LaCrescent. Trees begin bearing the third year and hit full production about year eight. Black knot is the disease to watch — remove infected branches in late winter and pick knot-resistant varieties (Toka, Obilinaja, Superior). Most rootstocks sucker heavily; keep the base clean.
crops.source: UMaine Bulletin #2034 Plum Production in Maine (varieties, rootstocks, spacing, pollination, black knot); Types of Fruit Trees for hardiness zones.

permanent.note: Full sun on a slope with air drainage — plums bloom early and the site is half the crop protection. Well-drained soil, pH 6.0-7.0, 12-18 ft spacing by rootstock. Permanent orchard tree; Japanese and European types must each be matched with their own kind for pollination.

crops.name: Sweet cherry
crops.label: sweet cherry tree

planting.note: not a bed crop — dwarf sweet cherries today, at 6-8 ft; standard trees are huge and difficult to net

bed30.note: dwarf sweet cherry 6-8 ft (spacing page); non-dwarf types get extra 5 ft beyond apples

crops.watch_for: spring frost on the earliest bloom of any fruit tree, brown rot on ripening fruit, cherry fruit fly maggots, birds — netting is mandatory or the tree is a bird feeder
crops.watering: Five gallons a week while establishing; keep soil even at fruit swell to reduce cracking.
crops.method_notes: HONESTY FIRST: sweet cherry is marginal in zone 5b. UMaine's zone guidance puts sweet cherries among the fruits that 'suffer winter injury in colder years' even in zone 5, and its cherry recommendations for a mild coastal 5b site steer to tart and duke cherries instead — the sweet cherry's early bloom is a standing invitation to frost, and it is the most disease-susceptible of the cherries. If you try one anyway in Wiscasset's coastal moderation: choose a self-fertile, late-blooming variety (Lapins, Stella, Sweetheart), on dwarfing rootstock so you can actually net it, on the warmest slope you have. Expect a crop roughly every other year. Otherwise, a tart or duke cherry is the honest, productive choice.
crops.source: UMaine Cooperative Extension: Types of Fruit Trees (hardiness zones, disease susceptibility); Ask the Expert: hardy sweet or tart cherry recommendations for a zone 5b Maine site.

permanent.note: MARGINAL in zone 5b: sweet cherries bloom earliest, suffer winter injury in cold years and need dwarf rootstock plus netting. Full sun, well-drained slope, 6-8 ft for dwarfs. Treat as an experiment here; a tart or duke cherry is the reliably productive choice.

crops.name: Tart (sour) cherry
crops.label: tart cherry tree

planting.note: not a bed crop — one tree; naturally a semidwarf tree at 15 ft spacing

bed30.note: semidwarf at about 15 ft, like a semidwarf apple

crops.watch_for: brown rot in wet weather as fruit ripens, cherry fruit fly maggots, birds (net); far less bothered by frost and disease than sweet cherry
crops.watering: Five gallons a week while establishing; even moisture at fruit swell to prevent cracking.
crops.method_notes: This is the honest cherry for zone 5b: naturally semidwarf (12-18 ft), genuinely winter hardy, self-fruitful, and tolerant of spring freezes that would destroy a sweet cherry crop. UMaine's coastal-Maine cherry recommendations are tart varieties — Carmine Jewel, Evans, Mesabi, Meteor, North Star — plus the duke hybrids (Balaton, May Duke, Almaden) which carry sweet-cherry flavor with sour-cherry hardiness. Plant in early spring, graft union above ground, open-center training for stone fruits. It blooms with or slightly after apples, still early, so give it a slope with air drainage. Fruit ripens late June-early July; pick before birds do and net if you want a full harvest. Trees begin to bear by year 3-4.
crops.source: UMaine Cooperative Extension: Ask the Expert cherry recommendations for zone 5b Maine (June 2022); Types of Fruit Trees (sour cherry hardiness and form).

permanent.note: Full sun, well-drained soil, air-drained slope. The hardy, productive cherry for zone 5b — a naturally semidwarf permanent tree, self-fruitful, renewed by annual dormant pruning. Outside the vegetable rotation.

crops.name: Peach
crops.label: peach tree

planting.note: not a bed crop — one tree at 15 ft, or 8 ft with annual pruning

bed30.note: 15 ft traditional spacing; 8 ft possible with annual pruning in Maine's cold-limited growth (UMaine)

crops.watch_for: peach leaf curl (the defining disease — Redhaven has good resistance, Reliance poor), brown rot on ripening fruit, peach tree borer at the trunk base, plum curculio; winter kills flower buds below about -10F
crops.watering: 2-5 gallons per tree during dry spells; mulch 3-4 in with wood chips, keeping it off the trunk (nothing that invites voles).
crops.method_notes: The honest truth from UMaine's peach specialist: peach trees in Maine live about seven years on average — severely cold winters can kill them at any age — and bloom mid-May, usually (but not always) escaping frost. This is a 'gamble that pays deliciously' crop in zone 5b, not a reliable one. If you plant: hardiest varieties only — Contender, Reliance, Redhaven, Cresthaven all have good flower-bud hardiness and were evaluated by UMaine at Highmoor Farm in zone 5b; Glowingstar and the donut peach BuenOsII are newer good-bud-hardiness picks. Site on a slope with air drainage, full sun, pH 6.0-7.0. Expect fewer fruit whenever winter dips below -10F; prune late (April, after cold passes) to preserve flower buds; thin fruit hard. Harvest late July through late September by spot-picking.
crops.source: UMaine Bulletin #2068 Growing Peaches in Maine (life expectancy, hardy varieties, site, pruning, harvest); Types of Fruit Trees (zone adaptability).

permanent.note: MARGINAL in zone 5b: UMaine puts lifetime expectancy at roughly 7 years in Maine, with winter bud kill below -10F the usual end. Needs full sun on an air-drained slope, pH 6.0-7.0. Plant the hardiest varieties and treat as a short-lived delight, not a long-term tree.

crops.name: Quince
crops.label: quince tree

planting.note: not a bed crop — one tree; naturally dwarf so it needs less space than most fruit trees

bed30.note: naturally dwarf tree, about 10 ft spacing

crops.watch_for: fire blight and quince rust (most varieties lack resistance — the honest risk), codling moth; flower buds damaged in severe winters
crops.watering: Regular water through establishment and fruit swell; mature trees tolerate dry spells.
crops.method_notes: Quince is a niche fruit with real limits in zone 5b. Per UMaine: most quince are hardy to zone 5 (-20F) and a few to zone 4, so Wiscasset sits at the edge of its range; fruit needs a LONG growing season, so on the coast (which buys us weeks of fall warmth) choose a short-season variety — Smyrna, Van Deman, Limon and Pineapple are the named ones. The honest warnings: nearly all varieties lack resistance to fire blight and quince rust (two diseases Maine's damp June weather encourages), and the fruit is rock-hard and astringent until cooked — it is strictly a jelly/preserve fruit. It is naturally dwarf, self-fruitful, and beautiful in flower, which is most people's real reason to grow it. Treat as a southern-Maine specialty, site warm, and don't count on it the way you'd count on an apple.
crops.source: UMaine Cooperative Extension, Types of Fruit Trees (quince hardiness, varieties, diseases); Fedco Trees availability for the named varieties.

permanent.note: MARGINAL but viable in zone 5b coastal sites. Naturally dwarf tree needing less room; hardy to roughly -20F. Needs a long, warm fall to ripen fruit and has weak disease resistance (fire blight, quince rust). A specimen/preserve fruit tree, not a production staple.

crops.name: Hazelnut (American filbert)
crops.label: hazelnut shrubs

planting.note: not a bed crop — one shrub per 4x8 at 10-15 ft spacing; plant more than one for nut set

bed30.note: 10-15 ft apart; a multi-stemmed shrub 12-18 ft tall and 10-15 ft wide

crops.watch_for: eastern filbert blight (the disease that kills European hazels — American hazelnut is resistant), nut weevil leaving 'hit' marks on shells, squirrels/deer/voles/small rodents in the harvest
crops.watering: Weekly water the first year until roots establish; after that, only in prolonged drought.
crops.method_notes: The easiest nut for Maine: the native American hazelnut (Corylus americana) is blight-resistant, cold hardy to zone 4, pH-adaptable, and unfussy about soil — UMaine's own Master Gardener article calls it the perfect low-maintenance native nut. It grows as a multi-stemmed shrub (or pruned to a small tree), so it belongs in a hedgerow, not a bed. Needs cross-pollination — plant at least two (Fedco: plant more than one, 4-6 ft apart for a thicket, or 10-15 ft for specimen shrubs), wind carries the pollen. First nuts 3-5 years after planting, then dependable 40-50 year yields — about the third week of September in central Maine, when husks turn brown. Protection for the first three years is the weak point: cage against deer and voles or they'll eat the young ones. Hybrids (Jefferson, zone 5) give bigger European-type nuts with EFB resistance.
crops.source: UMaine Home Garden News March 2022: American Hazelnut feature (hardiness, size, yields, harvest date, pests); Fedco Trees: American Hazelnut and Jefferson Hazelnut listings (spacing, culture).

permanent.note: American hazelnut: hardy zone 4, prefers well-drained soil but genuinely pH-adaptable, full sun for best nut set (light shade reduces yield). A multi-stemmed shrub 12-18 ft tall producing for 40-50 years. Needs a second plant for pollination; young plants must be caged from deer and voles for three years.

crops.name: Radish
crops.label: radish strip

planting.note: four 8 ft rows, sown 1 in apart, thinned to 1 in

bed30.note: four rows 6 in apart, thinned to 1 in — sown thick, pulled fast

crops.watch_for: flea beetles and cabbage root maggot — row cover at seeding keeps both out (NEVMG); hot, dry spells make roots pithy and pungent
crops.watering: Keep evenly moist; a dry spell mid-growth makes roots hot and pithy.
crops.method_notes: The fastest crop in the garden — NEVMG: 21–28 days, sow every ~10 days as a rotation, spring and fall only (summer heat ruins quality). Scatter a few seeds in slow-germinating carrot, beet and parsnip rows to mark them, a UMaine-published practice. No storage worth planning: pull as they size up.
crops.source: New England Vegetable Management Guide (UMass/UNH/UVM/UMaine): Radish crop + insect control pages (21–28 days, 10-day interval, row cover for flea beetles/root maggot); UMaine Cooperative Extension Maine Home Garden News April 2015 (row-marker practice); UMaine Bulletins #2190 (varieties) and Planting Chart for the Home Vegetable Garden (Lois Stack).

crops.name: Turnip
crops.label: turnip bed

planting.note: two 8 ft rows, seed 1 in apart, thin to 4–6 in

bed30.note: three rows 9 in apart, thinned to 6 in — turnips hate crowding

crops.watch_for: flea beetles on seedlings (a mid-July sowing skips the worst spring flush), cabbage root maggot, clubroot in brassica rotation
crops.watering: Even moisture; drought turns roots woody and bitter.
crops.method_notes: Fast and forgiving: spring crop as soon as ground is workable, plus a midsummer sowing for fall. Frost sweetens them, but MOFGA is explicit that turnips cannot withstand freezing — lift before hard freeze. Best pulled at 2–4 in; larger roots get fibrous. Greens are a harvest in their own right.
crops.source: MOFGA 'Grow Turnips' (R. Bailey, 2004, Maine); UMaine Cooperative Extension Planting Chart (Lois Stack) — seed 1/4–1/2 in deep, rows 12–18 in; NEVMG Rutabaga and Turnip Insect Control; UMaine Bulletin #2190 (varieties: Hakurei, Purple Top White Globe, Tokyo Cross); UNH Extension Planting & Maturity Dates of Vegetables in NH.

crops.name: Rutabaga
crops.label: rutabaga bed

planting.note: two 8 ft rows, seed 1 in apart, thin to 6–8 in

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart, thinned to 8 in for full-size roots

crops.watch_for: flea beetles on young plants (the reason Maine sows mid-June, after the first flush), cabbage root maggot, clubroot in brassica rotation
crops.watering: Deep taproot tolerates mild drought; water through late-summer dry spells while roots bulk.
crops.method_notes: The Maine fall storage root: sow mid-June per MOFGA to dodge flea beetles, harvest early October before the ground freezes — rutabagas withstand some freezing but are dug and stored cool and near-constant, not left in. Single sowing, no succession. One of the Coleman winter-table crops from storage, not from the bed.
crops.source: MOFGA 'Grow Turnips' (R. Bailey, 2004, Maine — 90–100 days, mid-June sowing, thin 6–8 in, store 32–38°F); NEVMG Rutabaga and Turnip Insect Control; Fedco Seeds (Laurentian); UMaine Bulletin #2190 (varieties: American Purple Top, Joan, Laurentian, York); UNH Extension Planting & Maturity Dates.

crops.name: Parsnip
crops.label: parsnip rows

planting.note: two 8 ft rows, seed 1 in apart, thin to 3 in

bed30.note: three rows 9 in apart, thinned to 3 in; deep, stone-free soil or roots fork

crops.watch_for: carrot rust fly — NEVMG notes it also attacks parsnips, mining the upper root; canker and forking in heavy or manured soil; parsnip seed barely keeps a year, sow fresh
crops.watering: Even, deep moisture all season; dry spells produce tough, cracked roots.
crops.method_notes: The classic in-ground winter root: UMaine Bulletin #4311 and Coleman's winter-harvest practice both leave parsnips to overwinter under mulch for sweeter spring roots (frost converts starch to sugar). Sow mid-to-late April in coastal Maine (UMaine planting chart; coastal dates run 10–14 days earlier than central). Single sowing. NOTE: NEVMG flags that over-wintered crops can harbor carrot rust fly larvae — weigh the trade and rotate beds.
crops.source: UMaine Cooperative Extension Bulletin #4311 (overwintering for a sweeter spring product); UMaine Planting Chart (Lois Stack) — rows 18–24 in, thin 2–4 in; NEVMG Carrot and Parsnip Insect Control (rust fly on parsnips, onion intercropping); Fedco Seeds (Harris Model, 120 days from direct seeding); UMaine Bulletin #2190 (Harris Model, Lancer).

crops.name: Celeriac
crops.label: celeriac row

planting.note: two 8 ft rows 12 in apart, plants 6–8 in apart

bed30.note: double rows 14 in apart, plants 6 in apart — UMaine Highmoor trials found 6 in yields most per bed-foot

crops.watch_for: leaf blight (Septoria) in humid spells, leafminers, aphids; black heart and cracked roots from uneven moisture — celery relatives need steady water
crops.watering: Consistent moisture all season; uneven watering cracks the root and brings black heart.
crops.method_notes: Slow, cool-season, worth it: start indoors ~10 weeks before last frost (UMaine seeded 13 Apr for a 22 Jun transplant), set out after frost, dig September–November before hard freeze — it is dug and stored, not a true winter-harvest root. UMaine Highmoor 2022 trial: 6 in in-row on double rows 14 in apart gave the greatest marketable yield per bed-foot (cultivars Brilliant, Balena best); 100+ days from transplant to mature. Stores 6–8 months near freezing — the winter stand-in for celery flavor.
crops.source: UMaine Cooperative Extension Highmoor Farm Celeriac Evaluation 2022 (Ginakes, Hutton, Handley — spacing trial, 121 days to harvest); MOFGA 'Celeriac' (100 days from transplant, 6–8 in spacing, 3–5 in harvest, storage); Johnny's Selected Seeds (Brilliant, 100 days from transplant); UMaine Bulletin #2190 (celery varieties Utah 52-70, Ventura).

crops.name: Sweet potato
crops.label: sweet potato row

planting.note: one 8 ft row, slips 12–15 in apart; vines will spill over the bed

bed30.note: one row down the middle on black plastic, slips 9–12 in apart; vines overrun the path by August — expected

crops.watch_for: voles (UNH: can eat an entire harvest), deer browsing the vines, scurf (harmless black skin patches), wireworms in ground that was recently sod
crops.watering: Water slips in well at planting; after that, little — overwatering fattens vines at the expense of roots.
crops.method_notes: Honest marginality in zone 5b: it works but only just. Needs 90–120 frost-free days AND warm soil — UNH's data put soil under black plastic at 65°F by June 1 in Durham; plant slips only once soil is above 65°F and use black plastic to buy weeks. Start slips from storage roots 6–8 weeks out, or order them; choose early UNH-tested varieties (Georgia Jet, Beauregard, Covington). Dig as late as possible but before hard frost (light frost on vines is fine); cure warm and humid for about a week, then hold cool — the exact curing figures are in the UNH fact sheet cited below. A cool, wet summer cuts yields hard — the most weather-dependent crop in this plan.
crops.source: UNH Cooperative Extension Fact Sheet 'Growing Sweetpotatoes in New Hampshire' (Sideman — 90–120 frost-free days, soil >65°F, 9–12 in spacing, black plastic, pests, curing); UNH NH Agricultural Experiment Station cultivar trials (Beauregard, Covington highest yields; MOFGA Pest Report 2013 summary); MOFGA sweet potato feature (Maine growers, first-week-of-June planting, 1 ft slips, harvest late Sept); UMaine Maine Home Garden News Oct 2025 (harvest & curing).
